title: Power BI reports support OAP exceptions for semantic models in separate workspaces (Preview)
text: Workspace outbound access protection (OAP) helps you control where data in a Microsoft Fabric workspace can flow. The initial preview for Power BI reports , launched in June, required a report in an OAP-protected workspace to use a semantic model in that same workspace. Customer feedback highlighted that this was too restrictive. With this improvement, a report can now query a semantic model in another workspace provided a workspace administrator explicitly allowed that destination through an OAP exception policy. Apply exception policies to allow report-to-model connections OAP continues to block outbound report-to-model connections by default. When a report opens, Power BI evaluates the report workspace policy before it renders the report in the browser. If the destination workspace is covered by an applicable exception, the report can connect to its semantic model. Otherwise, Power BI blocks the connection, and the report does not open. The report honors the policy that a workspace admin configured for the semantic model destination. You don't configure an exception on each report, and you don't need to move the report and semantic model into the same workspace. The OAP exception policy supports a common Power BI architecture: a central team manages shared semantic models in one workspace, while business teams build reports in separate workspaces. You can preserve that separation of ownership without removing the outbound boundary from the report workspace. See the improvement in action The following example shows a report stored in an OAP-protected workspace, and its semantic model is stored in another workspace. First, the report does not have an applicable exception policy. Power BI blocks the cross-workspace connection and displays the following error because the report can't access its semantic model. Figure: OAP continues to block outbound report-to-model connections by default. Next, a workspace admin creates an exception policy for the semantic model workspace. In the workspace settings under Outbound networking, select Add new cloud connection rule, select Power BI Semantic Model as the Connection Kind, and select the desired semantic model workspace under Workspace exception, as in the following screenshot. Select Add, and then select Save to save the Data Connection rules. Figure: An OAP exception policy to allow report-to-model connections. After the policy takes effect, the same report loads and its visuals render successfully. The report binding doesn't change. The OAP policy determines whether the cross-workspace connection is allowed. The semantic model remains subject to its own OAP controls. Connections from the semantic model to cloud databases, on-premises systems through gateways, lakehouses, warehouses, and other sources are still evaluated against the semantic model workspace's data connection rules . Make sure you enable OAP for both, the report workspace as well as for the semantic model workspace. Next steps Work with your workspace admin to confirm that your report workspace meets the OAP prerequisites and that OAP is enabled. Then create an exception policy for each approved semantic model destination. Policy changes can take about 15 minutes to propagate. For configuration details, refer to the Workspace outbound access protection for Power BI reports documentation. To understand downstream enforcement, refer to Workspace outbound access protection for semantic models .

title: Build more connected workflows with Fabric Actions and Business Actions in Fabric Pipelines (Preview)
text: Modern data workflows rarely stop at moving and transforming data. Once data is ready, you may need to trigger another operation in Fabric, refresh a semantic model, update a business application, send a notification, generate a document, or kick off the next step in a business process. With Fabric Actions and Business Actions activities in Microsoft Fabric Data Factory, you can bring these steps directly into your Fabric pipelines. Together, these activities make it easier to orchestrate workflows across Fabric and the business applications your organization relies on, without having to build and maintain custom API integrations for every scenario. We’re continuing to expand what you can do with these activities, with support for more Fabric operations and 25 additional third-party connectors for Business Actions. Bring Fabric operations directly into your pipelines The Fabric Actions activity lets you invoke supported Fabric REST API operations directly from a pipeline. Instead of manually constructing REST API requests and managing the underlying authentication and request details, you can select the Fabric operation you need, configure its inputs, and incorporate it into the rest of your pipeline workflow. We’re expanding the range of supported Fabric actions across experiences such as Lakehouse, Warehouse, Notebook, Copy Job, Dataflow, Eventhouse, Eventstream, semantic models, OneLake shortcuts, Workspaces, Capacity, and more. This gives you more ways to automate Fabric as part of an end-to-end workflow. For example, you could run a Notebook as part of your data processing flow, manage a OneLake shortcut, perform a Lakehouse operation, or refresh a semantic model after new data is ready, all orchestrated from the same pipeline. Fabric Actions also provides built-in connection and credential handling, helping reduce the authentication and integration work that would otherwise be required when calling supported Fabric APIs directly. The following visual shows how you can select and configure a Fabric operation directly within your pipeline. Figure: Invoke supported Fabric operations directly from your pipeline with Fabric Actions. Connect your pipelines to more business applications While Fabric Actions helps you orchestrate operations within Fabric, Business Actions helps connect your data workflows to the business applications and services where business processes happen. With this release, we’re expanding Business Actions with 25 additional third-party connectors, opening new possibilities across CRM, communications, document generation and signing, security, financial planning, project management, marketing, and more. For example, you can use Business Actions to: Send SMS notifications with D7SMS . Generate contracts, invoices, proposals, and other documents with Formstack Documents . Automate CRM and sales processes with connectors such as Pipeliner CRM and Commercient . Incorporate electronic signature workflows with Nitro Sign Enterprise Verified . Connect pipeline workflows with project and portfolio management systems. Integrate security and threat intelligence operations with services such as RiskIQ. Automate website content publishing with WP Connectr for WordPress . These additions build on the Business Actions experience to give pipeline authors more ways to connect data with the systems and processes that teams use every day. The following visual highlights some of the business applications that can be connected to your pipeline using Business Actions. Figure: Connect your pipelines to business applications and services with Business Actions. Find and configure the action you need As we expand the actions available to pipeline authors, we’re also making them easier to discover and configure. Discover Fabric operations With the updated Fabric Actions experience, you can browse or search for supported Fabric operations instead of needing to know the underlying REST API endpoint ahead of time. Once you select an operation, the activity surfaces the relevant configuration and required parameters. You can then select an existing Fabric connection or create one, provide the required inputs, and use dynamic content where supported. The following visual shows the updated experience for discovering the Fabric operation you want to use. Figure: Browse supported Fabric operations from the Fabric Actions picker. Figure: Search for supported Fabric operations from the Fabric Actions picker. Configure your action Getting started is straightforward. Add Fabric Actions or Business Actions to your pipeline, find the operation you want to perform, configure the required inputs and connection, and incorporate the activity into your pipeline flow. For Fabric Actions: Create or open a pipeline in Microsoft Fabric Data Factory. Add the Fabric Actions activity to the pipeline. Browse or search for the Fabric operation you want to perform. Select or create a Fabric connection. Configure the required inputs. Save and run your pipeline. When the activity runs, the selected Fabric operation executes as part of the pipeline, with its response available through the activity output. Business Actions follows the same principle by providing structured configuration for supported business application operations, so you can incorporate business processes without starting from a custom API integration. Go from data workflows to business workflows The real power comes from combining Fabric Actions and Business Actions with the rest of your pipeline. Consider a pipeline that processes the latest sales data. Once processing completes, the same pipeline could refresh the semantic model used for reporting, create or update a record in a CRM system, generate a customer document, and send a notification that the latest information is ready. Or imagine a document workflow where a pipeline processes business data, generates a contract from that data, starts an electronic signature process, and continues downstream processing once the appropriate business step has taken place. Rather than building separate integrations for each part of the process, you can bring data processing, Fabric operations, and business actions together as part of a larger orchestrated workflow. This allows your pipelines to coordinate not only what happens to your data, but what happens next because of your data. The following visual shows an example of an end-to-end pipeline that brings data processing, Fabric operations, and business processes together. Figure: Bring data, Fabric operations, and business actions together in a single pipeline. More actions, more possibilities We’re continuing to expand both Fabric Actions and Business Actions to give pipeline authors more ways to connect their data workflows with the next step in their business process. For Fabric Actions, that means broader coverage across Fabric workloads and platform operations, from Lakehouse, Warehouse, Notebook, and Copy Job to semantic models, OneLake shortcuts, Workspaces, Capacity, and more. For Business Actions, that means expanding the connector ecosystem so pipelines can interact with more of the applications and services organizations use every day. Our goal is to make these integrations easier to discover, configure, and incorporate into the pipelines you already build, so you can spend less time building integration plumbing and more time building end-to-end workflows. Get started To get started, open a pipeline in Microsoft Fabric Data Factory and explore the Fabric Actions and Business Actions activities. Whether you’re automating an operation within Fabric, connecting your pipeline to a downstream business application, or building a workflow that spans both, Fabric Actions and Business Actions give you more ways to turn data into action directly from Fabric Pipelines. title: Regular expression functions in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview)
text: Data warehouses routinely ingest valuable information embedded in free text, where inconsistent structure makes it difficult to query, connect, and analyze. Incoming values can also require quality checks before they reach curated tables. Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint now support scalar regular expression functions in preview, so you can extract useful values, validate formats, standardize text, and mask sensitive data directly in T-SQL instead of adding a separate processing step. What’s new in preview Regular expressions provide a concise way to recognize, extract, and transform complex text patterns that would otherwise require multiple string operations. The preview introduces the following scalar functions: REGEXP_LIKE : checks whether text matches a pattern. REGEXP_REPLACE : replaces matching text to clean, standardize, or mask values. REGEXP_SUBSTR : extracts a substring that matches a pattern. REGEXP_INSTR : returns the position of a matching substring. REGEXP_COUNT : counts pattern occurrences in a string. Use these functions during refinement to turn identifiers embedded in free text into structured values and to flag malformed records before they reach downstream systems. The following scenarios demonstrate both uses. Extract useful values from raw text In this fictional example, inbound customer emails land in bronze.EmailMessages. The Sender column contains a value such as “Avery Smith”, and an order reference such as “ORD-10293” may appear in the Subject column. REGEXP_SUBSTR extracts the sender’s name, email address, company identifier, and order number as structured values that can be related to curated customer, company, and order data. Figure: Extracting structured values from email message text. For “Avery Smith ”, the query returns “Avery Smith” as the Name, “avery@contoso.com” as the Email, and “contoso” as the Company. It also extracts the order number from the Subject column. Validate contact data before it reaches downstream systems Contact data in the silver.DimCustomer table can contain missing characters, extra spaces, or email addresses that do not follow the expected format. REGEXP_LIKE identifies records that fail the format check, so you can review, correct, or quarantine them before the dimension feeds reports, campaigns, and downstream applications. SELECT SourceCustomerId, EmailAddress FROM silver.DimCustomer WHERE NOT REGEXP_LIKE(EmailAddress, '^[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}$'); The query isolates email addresses that do not match the expected format so they can be reviewed, corrected, or quarantined before the customer dimension is released to downstream consumers. Conclusion Regular expression functions help turn hard-to-use text into structured, trustworthy warehouse data. You can extract sender, company, and order details from inbound emails and validate contact values during refinement, all with concise T-SQL close to the source. The result is information that is easier to connect, analyze, and trust. Explore the preview and learn how to use regular expression functions in Fabric Data Warehouse in the documentation. Share your scenarios and feedback with the Microsoft Fabric community on Reddit .

title: Use OneLake as native storage for Azure Databricks (Generally Available)
text: Organizations increasingly use Microsoft Fabric and Azure Databricks together so teams can choose the tools that best fit their data engineering, analytics, and AI workloads while working from a common data foundation. OneLake external-location support for Azure Databricks Unity Catalog is now Generally available from the Microsoft Fabric side, with OneLake Security enabled by default for Azure Databricks Storage items. With this integration, supported Unity Catalog-managed data can be stored directly in OneLake. To understand the setup and supported scenarios, Connect Azure Databricks to a OneLake external location . Why this matters Data teams often need Azure Databricks and Microsoft Fabric in the same architecture. Without a shared storage approach, organizations may create copies of the same data for different platforms, introduce pipelines whose primary purpose is synchronization, and manage access independently across multiple storage locations. Using OneLake as managed storage for supported Unity Catalog objects gives organizations a common physical data foundation while preserving flexibility in the services used above it. Azure Databricks continues to provide compute and Unity Catalog management, while OneLake provides the storage destination and Fabric-side data-access controls. What's new in this release This release builds on the Beta announcement , which introduced OneLake external-location support for Unity Catalog. OneLake Security is now enabled by default for Azure Databricks Storage items, giving administrators explicit control over which approved identities can discover, read, or write data in OneLake. The updated security experience helps platform teams move from testing connectivity to planning controlled adoption. Administrators can evaluate where Azure Databricks data should be stored and explicitly configure the identities and permissions required to access it. One shared data foundation, with flexibility above it Use OneLake as the storage foundation Azure Databricks workloads can create supported Unity Catalog-managed data directly in OneLake. A Unity Catalog external location points to an Azure Databricks Storage item in OneLake, and a catalog or schema can use that external location as managed storage. Control access explicitly OneLake Security is enabled by default for Azure Databricks Storage items. Administrators can assign discovery, read, or write permissions based on the access each identity requires. Continue using Unity Catalog-managed objects Teams can continue using Azure Databricks and Unity Catalog to create and manage supported managed tables, volumes, views, materialized views, and streaming tables. The objects remain managed through the Azure Databricks experience while their underlying supported data is stored in OneLake. Keep platform responsibilities clear Azure Databricks remains the environment for Databricks compute and Unity Catalog management. Microsoft Fabric provides the capacity-backed workspace and Azure Databricks Storage item, while OneLake provides the physical storage foundation and corresponding Fabric-side access controls. How it works Provision storage in Microsoft Fabric: Create a capacity-backed Fabric workspace and an Azure Databricks Storage item. The storage item provides the OneLake location used by the integration. Configure identity and access: Use an Access Connector for Azure Databricks with a managed identity, or an approved service principal. Grant the identity the required Fabric workspace or item access and configure the applicable OneLake Security permissions. Create the Unity Catalog connection: In Azure Databricks, create a storage credential for the approved identity, and then create a OneLake external location that points to the Azure Databricks Storage item. Create Unity Catalog objects: Configure a catalog or schema to use the OneLake external location as managed storage. Data written by supported Azure Databricks workloads is then stored directly in OneLake. Security and governance A shared data foundation does not create a single permission model. Access must be configured in both Azure Databricks and Microsoft Fabric so that users and workloads can reach only the objects and data they require. Use a managed identity or service principal approved for the workload. Grant only the required Fabric workspace or item permission. Configure the applicable OneLake Security role with the required discovery, read, or write permissions. Configure Unity Catalog permissions for the corresponding Databricks objects and validate end-to-end access before broader rollout. Keeping these responsibilities separate helps administrators apply least-privilege access on both sides. It also makes troubleshooting clearer because Databricks object permissions and OneLake data permissions can be evaluated independently. Get started Ready to use OneLake as managed storage for Azure Databricks Unity Catalog objects? Start with the Connect Azure Databricks to a OneLake external location tutorial and plan your deployment.

title: Power Query Corner: Finding and connecting to data in the new experience (Preview)
text: About this series This is the first in a six-part Power Query Corner series exploring the new Power Query experience. Each post takes a closer look at a different part of the experience, including what’s changing, why it matters, and how you can put it to work. Getting data doesn't always begin with a connector name. You might know which database to use, recognize a team-maintained Fabric item, want to return to a source from yesterday, or already have the query logic you need. A connector list is useful once you've decided how to connect. But choosing the right data often comes before that decision. We moved to a module-based approach so Get data can support those different starting points, rather than making every task begin with the same connector picker. The idea is simple: start with what you know, then follow the route that fits the task . Modules organize discovery, reconnection, and authoring around that idea. They don't remove the need to authenticate, select the right objects, inspect a preview, or maintain the query afterward. This first Power Query Corner issue follows a sales-report scenario in the new Power BI Desktop experience. It also uses clearly labeled Power Query Online examples to explain the wider design, then looks at the five most frequently reported Get Data problems and the work addressing them. The customer-feedback analysis draws on publicly available reports in our community forum thread , where we track feedback on the new Power Query experience. Choose a Get data route that matches your task Priya is preparing a regional sales review. A colleague offers a spreadsheet export, but the team also maintains sales data in Fabric. Before choosing Excel or another connector, she needs to decide whether to reuse that maintained item, return to a known source, or establish a new connection. A module is a task-focused view inside Get data. Home brings the available routes together; the other modules give each task room for its own search, context, and actions. In Desktop, that includes New, Recent data, OneLake catalog, Blank table, and Blank query. The names and choices offered depend on the product hosting Power Query. Figure: Home brings different starting points into one Get data experience. View more opens the corresponding full module; a source shortcut starts that source's connection flow. Official Desktop documentation screenshot. Source: Microsoft Learn Know the source? Keep the direct route. If Priya already has the required server, file location, or service URL, New remains the straightforward route: search for the connector or browse its category, then supply the required settings. Home can provide a shortcut without first opening the full list. Selecting a connector starts the connection workflow; it doesn't immediately load data. This matters for familiar work. The module-based approach isn't an instruction to browse every module before choosing a CSV file. It should preserve a direct path for someone who already knows the source. Know the business data? Discover the item first. If Priya knows the team maintains sales data but doesn't know its endpoint, OneLake catalog gives her a different starting point. She can find an item by its business context, then review its type, owner, location, and available endorsement or sensitivity information before deciding to connect. Imagine two items, both named Sales: one is in the team's maintained reporting location, while the other belongs to a personal test project. The name alone isn't enough. Catalog context helps Priya ask the right questions before she commits the report to a source. Endorsement is a useful signal, not a guarantee of suitability, and discovering an item does not grant permission to read it. The benefit is not merely another way to open the same dialog: it lets Priya choose an appropriate existing data item before looking up connection details or creating another export. To learn more, refer to the OneLake catalog overview for the catalog's broader discovery, governance, and security roles. Used it before, or need a small starting table? Recent data is the route back to a source Priya already recognizes. It avoids starting the decision again at the connector list, but a recent entry isn't a snapshot of the data or a guarantee that its location and permissions are unchanged. Blank table and Blank query answer a different question: what if the starting point isn't an external source? Priya might enter a small RegionCode-to-RegionName mapping in Blank table or paste a self-contained M expression into Blank query. M is Power Query's formula language. Entered values become part of the query; pasting a spreadsheet's values does not create a refreshable connection to that spreadsheet. Power Query Online examples, not Desktop capabilities The broader module design also accommodates finding a source by browsing the place where it lives. Recognizing an Azure resource or a SharePoint site is different from knowing its server address or file URL. Where those source-browsing experiences are offered, they can carry the user from a recognizable location to the contents they want. Browsing into a location and selecting it for a connection are different actions, and a file's contents are different from a folder's file list. Browse Azure, SharePoint browsing, and Upload is not currently available as modules in Power BI Desktop. They are part of Dataflow Gen2, and some are also available in Power BI web modeling; the available modules vary by host. There is no committed release date for these modules in Power BI Desktop. This module distinction should not be confused with the availability of individual Azure or SharePoint connectors through New. Search scope, filters, previews, and available actions depend on the browser and host. The useful principle is to support recognition and navigation where appropriate while retaining direct connector configuration. Dataflow Gen2 illustrates another distinction: reusing data is not the same as reusing query logic . OneLake catalog helps find a data item; My Queries holds personal M scripts; Shared queries (Preview) let authors import logic shared by others. For example, Priya could reuse an existing region-cleanup script in a dataflow instead of recreating those transformations. Importing shared logic creates an independent copy, not a live link to its original, and does not transfer credentials or destinations. To learn more, refer to the My Queries or Shared Queries documentation. Figure: Dataflow Gen2 example, not Power BI Desktop: My Queries is a personal library of query logic, distinct from recent sources and from the separate Shared queries module. This published Dataflow Gen2 screenshot illustrates why different tasks need different entry points. Source: Microsoft Learn Modules can also support tasks such as describing transformations with Copilot in Dataflow Gen2, subject to that feature's requirements. That does not make every Power Query Online module a Desktop capability. Use Get Data in Dataflow Gen2 for its supported entry points and Data sources in Power BI Desktop for Desktop. Try it: Choose and preview a sales source in Power BI Desktop or web modeling You can use the October 2026 release of Power BI Desktop or try Power BI web modeling today with an authorized source in a nonproduction report. In Desktop, enable the preview: navigate to File > Options and settings > Options > Preview features, select New Power Query experience, and select OK. title: Eventhouse support for OneLake security (Generally Available)
text: Security should be consistent wherever you query your data. With OneLake security, you can define access controls once, close to the data, and apply them across supported Microsoft Fabric engines without recreating your security rules for each experience. Today, we’re announcing the general availability of OneLake security support for Eventhouse external tables. When these external tables query data secured by OneLake security, they automatically enforce object-level, column-level, and row-level access controls. This extends the same centrally managed security model to KQL queries, helping you maintain consistent, end-to-end security and governance across analytics experiences. Lakehouse data with Eventhouse power The Eventhouse endpoint for Lakehouses provides a high-performance query layer over data stored in the Lakehouse, bringing the speed and scale of the Eventhouse engine to your existing data without requiring another copy. Because access remains governed by OneLake security, users get Eventhouse performance while your organization maintains a shared, centrally managed security model across Fabric. Object, column, and row level security Eventhouse support covers three levels of access control, allowing you to tailor access to the data users need. Object-level security: Control which underlying OneLake tables a user can access. Creating an external table in Eventhouse does not grant access to the secured data it references. Column-level security: Limit access to sensitive columns. Users can analyze the data they’re permitted to access without gaining access to protected fields. Row-level security: Filter table data using the rules defined in your OneLake security roles. Users querying an external table receive only the rows they’re authorized to read. These controls are applied automatically based on the querying user’s effective OneLake permissions. The external table provides a way to query the data and not a separate path around its security. Figure: When the user queries the data through Eventhouse, only rows for “United States” are returned, based on the user’s OneLake security rules. Get started To get started, use OneLake security roles to define access to your OneLake tables, and then query the secured data through the Eventhouse endpoint. Test the experience with a representative data consumer to confirm that table access, column restrictions, and row filters match your intended policies. For more information about defining access controls, refer to Table, column, and row-level security in OneLake . With Eventhouse support for OneLake security, teams can use KQL to analyze Lakehouse data with Eventhouse performance while preserving centrally managed access controls across Fabric.

title: Find expensive queries from Capacity Metrics (Generally Available)
text: When warehouse capacity usage spikes, you need to quickly understand what ran, which warehouse drove the usage, and which queries require investigation. The Monitor in warehouse action in the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app connects the capacity-level view directly to Warehouse Monitor. It opens the selected warehouse with the relevant time window already applied, eliminating manual correlation across monitoring experiences. Figure: Animated GIF - demonstrating how to navigate from a Capacity Metrics timepoint to Warehouse Monitor in four steps. Follow the activity into your warehouse Open Capacity Metrics: From the Compute page, select your capacity and review CU % over time. Capacity Units, or CUs, represent the compute consumption tracked for the capacity. Choose a timepoint : Select the usage increase you want to investigate, and then select Explore and open TimePoint Detail. Choose an operation window: Under Background operations for time range, select a supported warehouse query operation whose Start and End times cover the interval. Then select Monitor in warehouse. Explore Warehouse Monitor: Open Query history to review statements that ran during the selected interval. Access required: Access to the Capacity Metrics app and the Admin role in the workspace containing the warehouse. For supported operations and navigation, refer to the Monitor in warehouse documentation. Find the queries worth investigating Start with CPU time. Add the column through Column options and sort from highest to lowest. CPU time is the processor time allocated to an execution. It is not elapsed duration or the Capacity Units billed for an individual query. No single metric explains the complete workload. Review these columns together: Data scanned: Identify statements that read large volumes of data. Compare OneLake reads with local disk, and memory reads to understand caching behavior. Result cache hit: A value of 2 means the query reused a cached result, 1 means the execution created a result set cache, and 0 means result caching did not apply. Query text: Review joins, predicates, and filters for unnecessary scans or processing. Label: Connect statements to a workload, business process, or test variation. Is distributed: Separate distributed executions, represented by 1, from nondistributed requests, represented by 0. For queries with high CPU time or data scanned, select View similar runs to determine whether the behavior is recurring or isolated. Add Query Insights fields such as application, SQL pool, status, and error code to identify the originating workload and distinguish expensive successful executions from failed or interrupted ones. For field definitions, refer to the query execution history column reference documentation. Make the same correlation with AI The Data Warehouse operations skill in Skills for Fabric can correlate Capacity Metrics data with Query Insights activity for the same warehouse and time window, using your existing permissions. Example prompt: Investigate the capacity spike for my warehouse from 14:00 to 15:00 UTC on November 3, 2026. Identify queries with high CPU time or data scanned, explain why each query stands out, and suggest the next investigation step. Review the supporting metrics and query details before making tuning or workload-management decisions. Next steps Try Monitor in warehouse the next time you see a capacity usage increase. Start with CPU time and data scanned, compare similar runs, and use workload metadata to determine what drove the activity. For more guidance, refer to the Warehouse performance guidelines , query blocking troubleshooting , and Monitor T-SQL queries documentation.

title: OneLake table APIs: Now with Iceberg writes, plus richer table metadata (Preview)
text: OneLake table APIs already let Iceberg-compatible engines discover and read tables in Microsoft Fabric. Today we're taking the next step with two additions: Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) writes through the OneLake table endpoint, now available, and a new additional table metadata API, in preview, for adding descriptions and tags to tables and columns. Together, they make OneLake a place where any engine can not only read data, but also publish it, with the business context people and AI agents need to use it well. Write native Iceberg tables from the engines you already use Until now, the OneLake Iceberg endpoint supported read-only metadata operations. Now, IRC-compatible clients can create native Iceberg tables, commit new snapshots, and request short-lived storage credentials through the same endpoint they already use for reads. That means engines such as PyIceberg, Snowflake, and DuckDB can land results directly in OneLake using standard Iceberg tooling, with no custom connectors or copy jobs. Some of the supported Iceberg REST Catalog operations at the OneLake table endpoint include: Operation What it does Status List/get/check namespaces Discovers the schemas in a data item Available List/get/check tables Discovers tables and returns their Iceberg metadata Available Create table Creates a native Iceberg table in a schema New! Commit table updates Commits new snapshots and metadata changes to a native Iceberg table New! Drop table Removes a table and its data from OneLake New! Load table credentials Returns short-lived storage credentials for a table (credential vending) New! Writes are built for multi-engine environments. Commits use optimistic concurrency checks, so a conflicting update fails instead of silently overwriting a newer table state. Credential vending lets clients write data files without managing separate storage access. And because the tables live in OneLake, they're immediately discoverable by every tool connected to the catalog. Many industry partners are already building on this feature. Snowflake supports the OneLake table APIs through the catalog-linked database feature, which automatically discovers schemas and tables in a Fabric data item, so Snowflake users can read, create, and write Iceberg tables in OneLake. ClickHouse also announced that it now writes Iceberg tables directly to OneLake using these APIs. Add business context to tables and columns Data is only as useful as people's understanding of it. The new additional table metadata API (preview) lets you read and write descriptions and key-value tags for a table and its columns, for example to explain a table's business purpose, record its owning team, or describe how to interpret a column. It uses one common REST route, so you don't need a format-specific catalog API to do it. It also works through internal OneLake shortcuts: updates apply to the target table, so everyone sees the same context whether they read through the shortcut or the source. Explore more in the OneLake documentation Check out our documentation for more information. This includes end-to-end samples, from configuring PyIceberg, Snowflake, and DuckDB for writes and credential vending to a Python sample that updates table metadata safely. Start with the following resources: OneLake table APIs overview OneLake Iceberg metadata API Iceberg table API samples Read and write additional table metadata (preview) We want your feedback! Start writing Iceberg tables to OneLake and try the additional table metadata preview today and share your experience with us. Have feedback? Share your ideas and vote at the Fabric Ideas site and join the conversation in the Microsoft Fabric Community.

title: Govern Fabric connections with admin APIs and data connection policies (Preview)
text: Co-author: Abhishek Narain Protect continuity, understand connection risk, and set tenant-wide guardrails Imagine that the person who built a business-critical pipeline has left your organization. The connection still exists, but nobody is sure who can manage it or whether its credentials will keep working. What begins as a handover problem quickly becomes a governance question: who owns your connections, where do they lead, and which identities should be allowed to use them? Microsoft Fabric brings these questions together through two complementary capabilities: Admin connection APIs give tenant administrators visibility and ownership-management tools across connection types. Data connection policies set preventive controls for cloud connections. Together, they support a practical sequence: restore responsibility, understand your connections, then enforce the authentication boundaries your organization needs. From recovery to prevention Keep work moving when a connection owner leaves A departure should not leave a connection without someone who can maintain it. When an existing connection has a single owner, a Fabric tenant administrator can use the admin connection APIs to grant the Owner role to a responsible successor, another administrator, or an appropriate service principal. This restores the ability to manage the connection and establishes clear accountability during the handover. Use the admin connection APIs to review current access, assign a responsible successor as an Owner, update an existing assignment, and remove access that is no longer appropriate. The role-assignment endpoints support GET, POST, PATCH, and DELETE operations; refer to Admin Connections REST API reference for endpoint syntax and examples. Ownership is only part of continuity. Granting Owner does not transfer or renew OAuth credentials, confer permissions on the source system, or guarantee that dependent workloads will run. The incoming owner must check the connection requirements, update or reauthenticate credentials where needed, and validate the workloads that depend on it. Treat that validation as part of offboarding, not a task to postpone until something fails. See your connections, endpoints, and access clearly A tenant-wide inventory helps administrators find ownership gaps, unexpected access, and connections that may require review before they become operational issues. The admin APIs provide visibility across all connection types, including connections you do not own or have permission to manage. By comparison, the standard Manage connections and gateways experience does not provide a tenant-wide inventory, even for administrators. Use the tenant-wide connections endpoint to collect the complete inventory, including all paginated results. The response includes connection names and IDs, connectivity and connector types, endpoint paths, privacy levels, and credential or authentication-type metadata—but not secret values. Combine this information with current role assignments to identify unexpected access and endpoints or domains that require closer review. Recency data can help prioritize the review. Created, last-linked, and last-credentials-used timestamps answer different questions: last linked indicates when the connection configuration was most recently associated with a workload, while last credentials used provides a runtime signal. These timestamps do not provide a complete historical audit log, an automatic dependency map, or proof that an apparently idle connection is safe to delete. Confirm critical dependencies with workload owners before making changes. Figure: Animated GIF — Read-only Fabric Connection Inventory sample app showing illustrative data; no live tenant details or ownership changes are shown. This read-only demonstration uses a Python client to list tenant connections and inspect a connection role assignment. It does not change ownership. For the admin API endpoints and an example response, refer to List Connections (Admin) and List Connection Role Assignments (Admin) . Try a read-only connection inventory app For a hands-on inventory, refer to the Fabric Connection Inventory sample app . It uses the admin connection APIs to list tenant connections and their Owner and PendingOwner assignments, with search and filters for reviewing connector types, endpoints, and ownership results. It does not change connections, assign owners, or enforce policies. This is a single-tenant deployment template, not a hosted app that readers can sign into. To use it, an organization must deploy its own instance in a workspace that supports Fabric Apps (Preview), configure a single-tenant Microsoft Entra app, grant delegated Tenant.Read.All consent, and sign in with a Fabric administrator account. See the repository’s setup instructions. Illustrative API examples To inventory connections across the tenant, an administrator can make a read-only request: GET https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/v1/admin/connections Authorization: Bearer { "value": [ { "id": "11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111", "displayName": "ContosoConnection", "connectivityType": "ShareableCloud", "connectionDetails": { "type": "Web", "path": "https://www.contoso.com/" } } ] } If the response includes a continuationToken, use it to request the next page. For an ownership handoff, the following illustrative write request shows the payload for adding a user as an Owner. It was not part of the read-only GIF or the production test: POST https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/v1/admin/connections/11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111/roleAssignments Authorization: Bearer Content-Type: application/json { "principal": { "id": "22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222", "type": "User" }, "role": "Owner" } An ownership assignment may require the incoming owner to reauthenticate. It does not transfer credentials or guarantee that dependent workloads will run. Make approved authentication methods the rule An inventory shows how connections authenticate today. An authentication allowlist turns your organization’s requirements into a tenant-wide boundary for cloud connections. Instead of relying on every creator to make the same choice, you define the methods that policy permits. An authentication allowlist helps administrators reduce inconsistent or noncompliant authentication choices across cloud connections. In the Fabric admin portal, select Data Policies in the left navigation, then open the Authentication allowlist tab. Add the approved authentication methods, turn on Restrict to allowlist, and select Save. Review the tenant-wide confirmation before committing. Select methods that meet your organization’s requirements and are supported by the relevant connectors; no single method is universally available or appropriate. When enforcement is enabled, methods outside the allowlist fail policy evaluation for existing as well as new cloud connections. Enable this carefully, because it can disrupt existing workflows. That makes the inventory essential preparation: identify affected connections, agree on supported alternatives with their owners, and plan credential changes before enabling the restriction. These controls govern cloud connections; they are not a promise of coverage for every gateway, desktop client, or data path. Figure: Authentication allowlist example before enforcement. Restrict to allowlist is turned off, and Workspace identity is included as a sample entry. Define which Microsoft Entra tenants can authenticate connections An approved authentication method does not make every Microsoft Entra tenant acceptable. Organizations may also need to block connection authentication associated with unapproved tenants. The Tenant allowlist addresses this requirement by defining which Microsoft Entra tenants can be used for Entra-authenticated cloud connections, helping reduce the risk of authentication through unapproved tenant identities. On Tenant allowlist, select Add tenant ID and enter the approved tena

title: Bring your Fabric data into your next app with connectors
text: Most business applications start with data that already exists. Customer orders may live in a Fabric SQL database. Inventory history may be in a Lakehouse. Sales performance may already be modeled in Power BI. The opportunity is not to move that data again, but to turn trusted data into an experience that helps people make decisions and take action. Connectors in Fabric Apps shorten that path. They give an app a consistent way to work with Fabric data, so developers can spend less time on integration plumbing and more time building the experience users need. Connect to the Fabric data you already trust. Build the experience your users need. Keep the application close to the data and governance foundation already in place. Instead of beginning with infrastructure, start with the customer's need: What should this app help someone understand, decide, or do? From data to an application Imagine a large telecommunications provider operating thousands of cell sites and serving millions of customers. Network telemetry may stream into a Lakehouse; service-impact and incident data may live in a Fabric SQL database; and trusted availability and capacity measures may already be modeled in Power BI. A report can show where the service is degrading. But a network operations engineer may need to go further: Which sites and customers are affected? Is the issue driven by congestion, equipment, power, or an upstream dependency? What maintenance work or recent changes are associated with the site? Can I create or update an incident and route the next action from the same experience? This is where a Fabric App adds value. Connectors let the app combine governed network and operational data in one task-oriented experience for investigation, triage, and action. Architecture: Network operations app Figure: Fabric data remains the foundation; connectors bring network and operational context into a task-oriented Fabric App. Network telemetry remains in Fabric; operational records stay in their governed source; and trusted measures continue to come from the semantic model. The Fabric App brings those sources together so an engineer can move from a network signal to an informed operational action without reconstructing context across multiple tools. Choose the connector that matches the job Choose the connector that matches the Fabric item and the job the app needs to perform. Fabric Apps supports documented connector patterns for lakehouse SQL analytics endpoints, warehouses, SQL databases in Fabric, and Power BI semantic models. Fabric source Connector type Documented operations Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint fabric-sqlanalytics Read Warehouse fabric-warehouse Read, create, update, delete SQL database in Fabric fabric-sqldatabase Read, create, update, delete Power BI semantic model fabric-semanticmodel executeQuery Request only the operations the scenario needs. For example, a read-only inventory experience should not request write access. An operational app that updates a warehouse or SQL database should make that requirement explicit. Three real-world patterns Incident triage A telecommunications provider can build a network operations app on a Lakehouse, Fabric SQL database, and semantic model. An engineer can search for a cell site; review latency, congestion, availability, and impacted services; inspect recent maintenance or configuration changes; and create or update the operational incident from one experience. Value: The engineer moves from detecting service degradation to understanding impact and coordinating the next action without switching across disconnected monitoring and case-management views. Customer 360 for sellers A sales team may have accounts and order data in a warehouse, product signals in a Lakehouse, and trusted revenue measures in a semantic model. A Fabric App can organize this information around the account and add a tailored experience for exploration, notes, recommended next steps, or AI-assisted questions. Value: The app is designed around the seller’s job, not around the boundaries between data systems. Retail store operations from a semantic model Imagine a retailer such as Nordstrom with trusted sales, inventory, fulfillment, and customer-service measures already defined in a Power BI semantic model. A Fabric App can use that model as the analytical foundation for a store operations experience where a manager reviews daily performance, identifies products at risk of stocking out, investigates order or pickup delays, and coordinates the next action with the store team. Value: Store teams reuse trusted business measures and move from insight to action without recreating logic or switching across multiple reports and operational tools. Start with one focused workflow A good first app starts with a narrow, valuable job. The builder journey is: Create or initialize a Fabric Apps project. Identify the Fabric item behind the workflow. Add a connector with only the operations the app needs. Test with the permissions and data boundaries expected for users. For example, a read-only warehouse connection can expose governed site and service-impact data to the app: npx rayfin connector add \ --type fabric-warehouse \ --workspace-id YOUR_WORKSPACE_ID \ --item-id YOUR_WAREHOUSE_ITEM_ID \ --name network-operations \ --operations read The connector is added to the project configuration and can then be used through the generated connector interface. For complete syntax, supported operations, prerequisites, and current limitations, see Connect Fabric Apps to Fabric data . Build from the data you already trust Your most valuable business data is already in Microsoft Fabric. Connectors help you turn that data into focused applications that do more than display insight by helping you complete real business tasks. Get started with Fabric App and connect to your data .

title: Salesforce Data 360 integration with OneLake (Preview)
text: A customer reports a missing delivery. The service case is in Salesforce, while the shipping and returns records are in Microsoft Fabric. Before a team can decide what to do next, it needs to connect those two views of the same customer experience. For many organizations, answering questions like this still means exporting customer data, building ingestion pipelines, and maintaining another copy for analytics. Every additional handoff adds work for data teams and another dataset to secure and reconcile. Business teams wait for a complete picture while customer decisions move ahead. Zero-copy file sharing offers a different approach by making source data available where it is needed for analysis, without first building a separate ingestion copy. The data is always current. This makes it easier to connect customer context with the financial, operational, and product information that gives it meaning. Introducing Salesforce Data 360 integration with OneLake Salesforce Data 360 Integration with OneLake is now available in preview. Using OneLake Shortcuts, organizations can make Salesforce Data 360 data available in a Fabric and query them alongside enterprise data. Salesforce Data 360 remains the source, while Microsoft OneLake brings the analysis together. Those shortcuts reference the data in Salesforce Data 360 rather than importing a separate copy into the lakehouse. Further, the data is always current without requiring you to do any additional refresh. Teams can use the lakehouse, warehouse, and other Fabric Engines to explore customer data, join it with other enterprise tables, and develop analytics using familiar Fabric experiences, including SQL and Spark. Key benefits include: Less integration work. Reference shared Salesforce data without building and maintaining a separate ingestion pipeline just to make it available in Fabric. More complete business insight in real time. Bring customer cases, accounts, and opportunities represented in shared Data Lake Objects into analysis with orders, financial transactions, and operational records in real time. As data is available in Data 360, it is immediately available in OneLake. Once you have the data in OneLake, you can target the following use cases: Customer retention analysis using Spark. Use Fabric notebooks to prepare features from shared customer data and operational history for churn or propensity models, subject to the organization's data-use and access policies. Customer profitability Dashboards. Combine shared customer and account Data Lake Objects with financial data in OneLake to examine revenue, service costs, and margin together. Build Power BI reporting on an appropriately configured semantic model. Churn Prediction. OneLake is integrated with Microsoft Foundry. Salesforce Data 360 data can be used with Microsoft Foundry to build ML models to predict churn. Ask questions about your data. Build Ontologies with Salesforce Data 360 and ask questions using Data Agents that will respond to context established with Ontologies. Getting started Prerequisites You need Salesforce Data 360 access with the Data Cloud Architect permission set and an edition that supports data sharing. Identify the Data Lake Objects to share and prepare a Fabric workspace with a lakehouse and permission to create table shortcuts. Decide on an authentication method supported by the connection: Use organizational account for testing and prototyping. Use Service principal method for production applications. If you use a service principal, register the application in Microsoft Entra ID and prepare the required credential. Configure Salesforce Data 360 shortcuts Prepare the Salesforce share in Salesforce Data 360: Create a data share containing the required Data Lake Objects. Create a Microsoft OneLake data share target using the Microsoft Entra tenant ID and the appropriate identity's object ID, then link the share to that target. Figure: Creating a data share in Salesforce Data 360 Create a Shortcut in Fabric: In the destination lakehouse, select Get data > New table shortcut > Salesforce Data 360. Use the target's Tenant Endpoint as the Salesforce instance URL and its Core Tenant ID as the Salesforce org ID, then configure authentication. Choose the shared Data Lake Objects, save the shortcuts, and query a selected object. Confirm that the target is linked in Salesforce and test access with the intended Fabric users and workloads. Figure: Creating a Salesforce Data 360 shortcut using the share During preview, only Data Lake Objects with the _dll extension is supported. Data Model Objects, Calculated Insight Objects, and schema-level shortcuts are not supported. We are excited to see what you build Salesforce Data 360 Integration with OneLake brings customer context closer to the enterprise data that helps teams act on it. By replacing a separate ingestion step with shared access through shortcuts, organizations can simplify the path from a business question to analysis while making access boundaries explicit. This integration advances the Microsoft Fabric and OneLake vision: make data easier to use together without requiring every source to move into one place. Salesforce Data 360 Shortcuts documentation provides you detailed information to get started. Share your feedback and use cases in the Microsoft Fabric Community . Your experience will help shape what comes next as we continue connecting customer data with enterprise analytics.

title: Share data and context across organizations with IQ Share (Preview)
text: The data needed to answer a business question rarely belongs to one organization. Enterprises depend on suppliers, software providers, research partners, and customers for information that complement their own. Yet getting that data into their workflow often means building another pipeline, maintaining another copy, and reconciling access across organizational boundaries. Even when the data arrives, its meaning can be left behind. Definitions, assumptions, and usage guidance are shared separately, leaving teams to reconstruct the context before they can put the data to work. With IQ Share in Microsoft Fabric, now in preview, organizations can share supported Fabric data items, along with context stored in lakehouse files, with recipients in other Fabric tenants. Data stays in the producer's tenant, recipients work in their own Fabric workspace, and producers retain control over access. Introducing IQ Share IQ Share brings cross-tenant data and context sharing into a Fabric item-based experience. In this preview, producers can share an entire Lakehouse, Warehouse, and Mirrored Items. For Lakehouses, markdown files can accompany the data with descriptions, business definitions, and instructions that help recipients understand how to use it. Key Benefits Zero-copy sharing. There are no data copies made. Data resides in the data producer’s tenant and shortcuts are created, allowing customers to get access to real time data and insights. Collaborate across tenants without provisioning a recipient identity in the producer's tenant. Keep shared data connected to its source. Newly added tables in a shared item are automatically reflected for consumers, without a separate export-and-refresh pipeline for the sharing relationship. Share meaning alongside data. Include Markdown context files in a Lakehouse so recipients can interpret the data and use that guidance when configuring downstream analytics or AI experiences. Manage access through the Share Lifecycle. Producers can review recipient acceptance, revoke access, and configure an expiration date that ends access automatically. They can centrally monitor all the shares from OneLake Catalog. API and CI/CD support is available for creating and accepting Shares. Use cases IQ Share can help organizations make partner data usable without replicating data. Enterprise scenarios include: Supplier and manufacturer collaboration: Share a curated inventory so a manufacturing partner can analyze supplier data alongside its own production information. Data-provider distribution: Deliver a curated lakehouse or warehouse to authorized customers in their Fabric tenants, with accompanying definitions were provided through lakehouse files. Joint financial analysis: Share an approved lakehouse with an external advisory team for a time-bound engagement, while the producer manages recipient access and expiration. Research collaboration: Share a curated research lakehouse and its data dictionary with another institution, helping researchers combine complementary information across tenants. Partner Integrations using IQ Share IQ Share allows partners like EY, TomTom, S&P Global, Financial Fabric, and xMentium to build integrations. TomTom, for example, is bringing its geospatial and transportation intelligence into Fabric through IQ sharing, with available data products discoverable through the OneLake catalog. These integrations will be available soon in OneLake Catalog. How IQShare works Terminology Figure: IQ Share Terminology and their descriptions Create and accepting a Share The producer selects a Lakehouse or Warehouse, adds recipients, and sets an expiration. IQ Share generates an invitation that you can share with the consumer. Each invited recipient reviews the Share and selects a destination workspace. Fabric creates a Share Subscription Item and a Mirrored OneLake Item for each shared source item. Mirrored OneLake Item is a read-only item that has Shortcuts to the data. Figure: Illustration of how Share and Share Subscription enables cross tenant sharing. Fabric-managed shortcuts reference the producer's data; no guest identity is required in the producer's tenant. Lakehouse Markdown files can supply definitions and usage guidance alongside the data. New tables added or deleted within an already shared item are automatically reflected for consumers. These source changes do not require a separate export pipeline. Adding or removing an entire item reflects on the consumer tenant when consumers refresh Share Subscription. Managing Shares You can add recipients anytime or update a share expiration. A configured expiration automatically ends access. Producers can also revoke a recipient or delete the Share. Getting started Prerequisites In the producer tenant, a Fabric administrator must enable Enable Share Item (Preview) and External data sharing tenant setting. In the consumer tenant, an administrator must enable Enable Share Subscription Item (Preview). The producer needs Read and Reshare permissions on the source item. The accepting user needs Contributor access to the destination workspace and must sign in with the identity added to the Share. Create an IQ Share In the producer workspace, select New item, then Share (Preview). Name the Share, select the lakehouse or warehouse, add recipients, and configure an expiration if appropriate. Review the selection, create the Share, and send the Share URL to the intended recipients. Figure: Creating a new IQ Share Accept an IQ Share Recipients uses the invitation URL to review the producer’s tenant information, shared content, and expiration, choose a destination workspace, and select Accept and create item. The resulting Share Subscription Item shows the relationship and shared-item status. Use the SQL endpoint to query the shared data. Spark notebooks, semantic models, data agents, and ontologies currently require an intermediate Lakehouse and shortcuts rather than direct use of the Mirrored OneLake Item. Figure: Accepting an IQ Share Security and governance considerations IQ Share shares the whole item, including newly added tables, so review both its current contents and future additions. Confirm recipient identities and organizational sharing policies before sending an invitation. Plan for lifecycle changes. Revocation, expiration, deletion of the Share, or loss of the Share creator's source access can interrupt consumer access and downstream dependencies. Review acceptance and status in the Share Item, document ownership, and test the end-to-end lifecycle with non-production data. We are excited to see what you build IQ Share helps organizations spend less time moving data across boundaries and more time using it together. By bringing whole-item sharing, recipient authorization, and access lifecycle controls into Microsoft Fabric, it simplifies collaboration while keeping the producer in control of the sharing relationship. Learn more about IQ Share refer to the documentation. Try the preview with a curated, nonproduction data product and share your feedback through the Microsoft Fabric Community . Your input will help shape the experience as we advance OneLake's vision of a unified data foundation where organizations can bring data and context together for analytics and AI.

title: Announcing support for Materialized views and streaming tables in Mirrored Azure Databricks catalog
text: Access more Unity Catalog objects through the existing mirrored catalog experience in Microsoft Fabric We are expanding Mirrored Azure Databricks catalogs in Microsoft Fabric to support materialized views and streaming tables alongside tables. These objects remain created and managed in Azure Databricks, while Fabric provides read-only access to the underlying data through shortcuts. This brings more of your Unity Catalog environment into Fabric without copying or replicating the data. What's new A Mirrored Azure Databricks catalog can now include support: Tables Materialized views Streaming tables When configuring the mirrored catalog, select the Unity Catalog catalogs, schemas, and supported objects you want to make available in Fabric. Fabric mirrors the selected catalog structure and creates shortcuts to the underlying data. This enhancement uses the existing Mirrored Azure Databricks catalog item and configuration workflow. There is no separate Fabric item type for materialized views or streaming tables. Why this matters Materialized views store precomputed results that can simplify recurring analytical queries. Streaming tables continuously process incoming data and maintain updated results for scenarios that require fresher information. Both object types can play an important role in the datasets that organizations publish for analytics and reporting. Supporting these objects in a mirrored catalog gives Fabric users access to more of the curated data already available in Azure Databricks. It also allows platform teams to preserve clear ownership: Azure Databricks remains responsible for creating and processing the source objects, while Fabric provides experiences for discovering and analyzing the available data. Prepare objects for external access Before a materialized view or streaming table can appear in Fabric, configure it for external data access in Azure Databricks, complete the applicable prerequisites, and grant the required Unity Catalog permissions to the identity used by Fabric. Then refresh or synchronize the mirrored catalog. Work with data in Fabric The mirrored catalog includes an automatically generated SQL analytics endpoint for exploring and querying the available data with T-SQL. You can also create a Power BI semantic model and use Direct Lake mode for reporting. Keep catalog changes in sync For new mirrors, automatic synchronization of future catalog changes for the selected schema is enabled by default. Supported additions and deletions of schemas, tables, materialized views, and streaming tables can be reflected in Fabric when they meet the configured selection and external-access requirements. Get started Follow Tutorial: Configure Microsoft Fabric mirror from Azure Databricks Unity Catalog to create or configure your mirrored catalog. Review Microsoft Fabric Mirrored Catalog from Azure Databricks for prerequisites and external-access guidance.

title: Adding the Context Streaming Events Need: Reference Data Joins with OneLake Delta Tables in Fabric Eventstream
text: Enrich events with business context in real time, enabling faster decisions, more relevant alerts, and lower operational effort downstream. A real-time event tells you what happened. Context tells you what it means—and what to do next. In cold-chain logistics, a temperature reading becomes actionable when paired with a shipment’s temperature limits, customer priority, and response contacts. Reference Data Join in Fabric Eventstream brings that context to live events by matching them with business information from Delta tables in OneLake before they reach downstream destinations—so consumers can understand and act on the events without performing separate lookups. The scenario: Cold chain logistics Cold chain logistics moves temperature-sensitive goods, such as fresh produce, dairy, frozen foods, and pharmaceuticals, from origin to destination within strict temperature ranges. Refrigerated trailers, containers, and warehouses must keep products in range at every stage. A few degrees off for too long can spoil a shipment, break compliance requirements, or put patient safety at risk. Refrigerated fleet continuously stream sensor telemetry. But a reading alone does not identify the shipment, its temperature limits, or the team responsible for responding. An alert without the context An alert arrives from a refrigerated trailer: " Device TRL-4471 reported 9.2°C. " Is the cargo at risk? Which customer is affected? Who should respond? The reading alone can't tell you. Figure: A raw temperature alert does not provide enough business context for immediate action. The missing context --assets, shipments, routes, customers, and response contact already lives in Delta tables in OneLake. Reference Data Join brings that information into Fabric Eventstream before events reach downstream consumers. In this illustrative scenario, the trailer carries fresh produce with a configured transport range of 2–8°C for this shipment. A 9.2°C reading is therefore an excursion that operators can assess using the shipment details and assigned response team. The pattern is simple: combine live events with business context, then let downstream rules and workflows decide who needs to act. For example, “TRL-4471: 9.2°C” becomes “Trailer TR-0918: 9.2°C; fresh produce; transport range 2–8°C; Northwind Foods; Tier 1; assigned response contacts.” A downstream rule can compare the reading with the shipment’s limits, flag the excursion, and notify the relevant team. The common workaround and tradeoffs Reference data can be joined either while events are in motion or after they land in a store. The right choice depends on when the business needs context. Land events first, then join for analytics. This approach keeps event payloads lean and avoids duplicating reference attributes on every record. It works well when analysis can wait until the data reaches downstream where it will be enriched. However, it adds a processing step and delays context that stream-based alerts, routing, and automated actions need immediately. Enrich events in the stream for time-sensitive scenarios. When alerts, routing, or automated actions must happen in real time, enriching events in motion provides the business context needed to respond immediately. It also creates complete, denormalized events that downstream consumers can use without repeating the join. The trade-off is larger payloads and duplicated reference values, which can increase transport and storage costs and require careful handling as reference data changes. For cold-chain monitoring, stream analytics is critical because a temperature excursion can require action before the event reaches storage. Enriching telemetry in Eventstream gives downstream detection and response workflows the cargo limits, customer priority, route, and contact context needed to assess the event immediately. If the use case is historical reporting rather than time-sensitive intervention, joining after ingestion may be the better design. Introducing Reference Data Join In Fabric Eventstream Reference Data Join lets you join a live stream with reference data stored as Delta tables in OneLake. The reference data appears as its own node on the Eventstream canvas. You join it to your stream inside the pipeline, before the data reaches any destination. Use OneLake Delta tables. Reuse master data exposed through a Lakehouse, including native tables and shortcuts to data in other workspaces, without copying the data. Choose no-code or SQL joins . Map keys visually for simple lookups or write SQL for advanced logic. Select inner or left outer joins . Keep the matching events for downstream processing or preserve every event and flag missing reference data. Add multiple reference data nodes . Add all the required context to the stream by adding one or more reference data nodes to the topology. Preview and validate on the canvas . Inspect reference rows and joined output before publishing. Control columns and refresh intervals . Load only the columns you need and keep slowly changing reference data current by configuring the refresh interval. Building the pipeline in few simple steps Using the cold-chain logistics scenario, we’ll build a real-time pipeline that enriches raw trailer telemetry with Reference Data Join. In this example, an eventstream receives live TrailerTelemetry events from Azure IoT Hub, joined with reference data in Onelake, and sends the enriched records downstream. The following steps show the core pattern; the linked Microsoft Learn guide provides the full setup instructions. Add the reference data node. In Edit mode, select Add source and choose Reference Data. A new node appears on the canvas next to your live stream. Figure: Add a Reference Data source to the Eventstream canvas. Point it to a Delta table in OneLake . Select the Lakehouse that exposes the reference data, then choose the Delta table you want to use. The table can be: Natively stored in the selected Lakehouse. A shortcut to a Delta table stored elsewhere in OneLake. Figure: Select the Lakehouse that exposes the reference data. Figure: Choose the Delta table to use as the reference source. 3. Load only the columns the pipeline needs and preview the data. After selecting the required columns, open the data preview to confirm the schema and check a few rows. In this illustrative shipment, TRL-4471 carries fresh produce with a specified transport range of 2–8°C for a Tier 1 grocery customer. That makes a 9.2°C reading an excursion requiring prompt assessment. Figure: Preview the reference-data schema and sample rows before joining. 4. Join it with the default stream. Connect the default stream and the reference node to a join operator. Map the key columns and choose a left outer join when you need to retain readings from devices missing in the reference table; choose an inner join when only matched events should continue. Use the SQL operator for more advanced logic. Figure: Configure the join between live telemetry and reference data. 5. Test and publish. Preview the enriched output on the canvas, then publish and route it to Eventhouse, Lakehouse, Activator or any other supported destination. As shown in the diagram, you can incorporate multiple reference data sources by chaining Reference Data nodes with join operators. Figure: Test, publish, and route the enriched stream to downstream destinations. Going further: SQL for advanced logic As needs grow, you may want logic beyond a simple lookup. For example, you might calculate an "out of range" flag in the stream and tag each event with the regional hub that covers the trailer's route. Add a SQL operator to your Eventstream topology and connect both the reference data nodes and the default stream to the input connector of the SQL operator node as shown in the figure below.
