title: OneLake: The file system for agent-first data engineering
text: Software engineers are increasingly using agents to build software, and data engineers are no different. We want OneLake to help enable data engineers to develop software in this new agent-first era. Think about how you work in a terminal: you use it to run programs that read and write files. Both the programs and the data live in the file system. Now apply that model to data engineering: OneLake is the file system, Fabric engines are the programs, and the AI prompt is your terminal. Over the last few weeks, we’ve released several new capabilities in OneLake that come together to create an experience where agent-first data engineers can thrive. This blog post provides a rundown of those features. Managing OneLake OneLake now offers a remotely hosted MCP server (preview), so agents can explore and manage your data without installing a local server. The local MCP option remains available if you prefer. We’ve also added tools to the Fabric Core MCP server for managing shortcuts and OneLake security . In our previous post , we asked an agent to document an open mirrored database. It found the workspace, discovered the table schema, mapped the underlying files, and checked replication health—all from a single prompt. That same scenario is now possible through the hosted OneLake MCP server. Once connected, ask: “Document what’s in the House Price Open Mirror in my UK Property Data workspace.” Figure: GitHub Copilot documents the House Price Open Mirror by using OneLake table and file tools. The agent uses OneLake’s table and file tools to explore the database and build its response, working within your existing permissions. The experience is the same; there’s simply no local server to install or maintain. The addition of the OneLake security tools extends what you can include in the documentation: “Use the Fabric MCP server to document the OneLake security rules of the PricePaid table in the InlandRevenueHousePriceData mirror” Figure: GitHub Copilot documents the OneLake security roles and permissions applied to the PricePaid table. Querying OneLake Agents need more than access to data—they need to know how best to query it. How do you turn a natural-language question into a query that works with data anywhere in OneLake? Continuing the house-price scenario, suppose you ask of the inland revenue database: Question: “Using the InlandRevenue mirrored item from the TomDemo workspace, tell me how many houses were sold in Hampshire in 2020?” Answer: “18,193 houses were sold in Hampshire in 2020, counting detached, semi-detached, and terraced houses. Including flats and maisonettes, the total was 21,452.” How does the agent know how to answer this question just by asking OneLake? Endpoint discovery. OneLake now provides an endpoint discovery API (Preview) that describes the Fabric Native engines available for each item and how to connect to them through skills, MCP servers, or engine-specific endpoints. The API also returns the OneLake Table APIs and File APIs so any agent can connect to the underlying data either directly or through tools like DuckDB . When you include a simple instruction to use the discovery API and load the returned skill for the default engine, GitHub Copilot in VSCode turns a natural-language question into a query tailored to that engine. Figure: GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code uses endpoint discovery to identify how to query the mirrored data. To query data through OneLake, the data doesn’t have to live in OneLake. Shortcuts allow you to query data anywhere without making a copy. Shortcut transforms allow you to convert data files into tables without writing a single line of code to create or maintain the tables as the files change. To continue the property price example, let’s combine the data from our mirrored database with some data in SharePoint. Mirrored databases are read-only, so here we’ll create a new Lakehouse to bring together our data and run a query: “Please follow these steps using the Fabric and OneLake MCP tools: Using my existing SharePoint connection, you’ll find a folder in my OneDrive https://onedrive.cloud.microsoft/xxx/Documents/SampleData/council-tax-2026-27 that contains CSV data, can you create a new Lakehouse in the TomDemo workspace with a shortcut to this CSV, please use a shortcut transform to turn this CSV into a table. Create another shortcut to the Inland Revenue PricePaid table. Answer this question: What is the most expensive tax Band D, where is it, and how many homes were sold each year since 2000 in those postcodes?” Answer: “Dorset has the highest 2026–27 Band D charge in the dataset: £2,765.02 annually, shared across 13,275 postcodes.” Below is the Lakehouse that was built containing a delta table of our CSV data and the result of the query: Figure: Lakehouse containing shortcuts to the council tax data and the Inland Revenue PricePaid table. Figure: GitHub Copilot returns annual home sales for the postcodes with the highest Band D council tax charge. Because this is a Lakehouse, it exposes a Spark endpoint, which allows us to run an analysis to check if there is any correlation between the median house price of an area and its council tax band. GitHub Copilot picks the Spark CLI skill returned by the discovery API to perform this analysis: Question: “now use the spark endpoint to run a spark job to see if median house price is correlated to the council tax band of the area - e.g., do higher tax bands have more expensive houses. Start with a Pearson correlation.” Answer: “The Spark job found a negative Pearson correlation: r = −0.562. Councils with higher Band D charges tended to have lower, not higher, median house sale prices.” Figure: GitHub Copilot uses the Spark CLI skill to run a Pearson correlation analysis in the Lakehouse. Figure: The analysis shows a negative correlation between Band D council tax charges and median house sale prices. Now, all that’s left to do is check the results! title: Modernize data integration strategy with Microsoft Fabric when using Snowflake and Databricks
text: Challenges solved by Microsoft Fabric Microsoft Fabric is an end-to-end analytics platform that brings together data integration, data engineering, warehousing, real-time analytics, business intelligence, and AI-related experiences. It has grown tremendously within the community because it is solving a key problem: lowering the integration tax across data and analytics systems. To understand the integration tax, consider a mid-sized or large organization that wants to perform analytics and data processing. It may use several source systems, an analytics platform such as a warehouse or lakehouse, and yet another platform or vendor for orchestration. To generate insights, the organization must integrate these different systems (hence the term integration tax). Fabric brings together a broad set of analytics capabilities within one platform, which can reduce the number of separate integrations an organization needs to design and operate. You can bring data into Fabric, store it in a warehouse or lakehouse, query and analyze it with Spark or T-SQL, visualize insights with Power BI, and support real-time scenarios with Real-Time Intelligence. Fabric also interoperates with platforms such as Snowflake and Databricks, helping organizations unify data and analytics across technologies while minimizing data movement and duplication. The following diagram shows how these experiences come together as part of the Microsoft Fabric platform. Figure: Microsoft Fabric brings data, analytics, AI, OneLake, and governance capabilities together on a unified platform. OneLake serves as Fabric's unified logical data layer. Fabric-managed data resides in OneLake, while shortcuts and some mirroring scenarios can reference data that remains outside OneLake. If one team owns the data and another team in the organization needs access, the second team does not need to duplicate it. Instead, it can create a Fabric shortcut and work with the same copy of the data. Beyond storage, OneLake also enables data-sharing and governance patterns across domains and workspaces. Organizations can expose data through shortcuts while maintaining ownership within the producing team, enabling data mesh architecture without duplicating datasets. Integration options We have discussed shortcuts briefly. Now let's look at how they work and at the other options available for making data accessible in Fabric: Shortcuts : Fabric lets you create a pointer to data in its existing location and access it without moving it. A shortcut is similar to a symbolic link or a Windows shortcut: the data source can differ from the location where users access it. For example, data can remain in Amazon S3 while a Fabric shortcut provides access to the required data. To users, the data appears to reside in Fabric even though it is retrieved from S3. Shortcut transformations also support selected transformations on shortcut data. Mirroring : For supported data sources, mirroring provides you with a low latency option to bring your data into Fabric. Depending on the source system, mirroring either continuously replicates data into OneLake or exposes the source through metadata mirroring and shortcuts. This approach reduces the need to manage pipelines or infrastructure and can offload analytical workloads from the source system. For example, if source data resides in an on-premises SQL Server database, you can create a SQL Server mirror in Fabric and analyze the latest available data there. Open Mirroring : This is an extension of mirroring for any data sources that are specific to your organization. Open Mirroring enables applications or partners to write changes directly into an open mirroring landing zone, after which Fabric converts and manages the data as Delta tables. Pipelines : are an option when a solution requires explicit data movement, multi-step orchestration, complex transformations, or integration across multiple sources. The following diagram illustrates how mirroring and shortcuts complement Fabric compute experiences by either bringing data into Fabric or making externally stored data available without traditional ingestion. Figure: Mirroring and shortcuts provide different approaches for making source data available to Fabric workloads. title: Bring insights and action together with Fabric Apps in Org apps
text: Business users move from understanding what happened, to investigating why, to acting. Microsoft Fabric can bring that journey together. Fabric Apps provide purpose-built, data-driven experiences when users need more than a report. Org apps distribute them alongside Power BI reports and other supported Fabric content in a curated destination. Move from insight to action in one destination Power BI reports help users monitor performance, explore trends, and understand what’s happening in the business. Many insights, however, lead to a next step: submitting a request, updating a plan, investigating an exception, assigning an owner, or tracking a resolution. A Fabric App provides the custom interface and workflow for that next step. Including it in an org app places action beside the reports and operational content that provide context. Users enter one destination organized around their role, review the insight, open the Fabric App, and act. Understanding apps in Fabric Experience Purpose Value Fabric Apps Build for a specific task Create purpose-built applications connected to Fabric data, with managed APIs, authentication, hosting, and service integration. Org apps Distribute in business context Package Fabric Apps with Power BI reports, paginated reports, notebooks, maps, and real-time dashboards, with tailored navigation, branding, and audiences. Workspace apps Distribute Power BI content Package and publish reports and dashboards from a workspace. Does not support notebooks and real-time dashboards, automatically granting and revoking access to underlying items and support for Fabric Git integration What the combined experience looks like Consider a retailer that wants regional managers to identify store issues and coordinate a response. The Store Performance page displays a Power BI report, with other business experiences available through the org app navigation. Start with the insight A regional manager opens the Retail Operations Hub , an app designed around the work of running stores. The landing experience surfaces a Power BI report with revenue, margin, inventory, and customer-service trends. A real-time dashboard highlights emerging operational issues. Figure: Shows a Power BI report with revenue, margin, inventory, and customer-service trends Continue into a Fabric App The report shows that a store is missing its sales target while carrying excess inventory. The manager opens the Store Action Planner , a Fabric App included in the same org app. The application brings the relevant context into a focused workflow where the manager can review the exception, choose a response, assign owners, and track the plan. Figure: The Store Action Planner opens as a dedicated Fabric App page within the Retail Operations Hub. Keep reporting and actions connected The org app keeps the solution together while tailoring content for regional and store managers. Business owners can update navigation and included items without rebuilding the Fabric App. Each team retains clear ownership: BI authors evolve reports, developers improve the Fabric App, and business owners curate the org app. Benefits One place to work: Move from Power BI insight to action without finding another tool. Role-based distribution: Give each audience the right mix of reports, applications, and operational content. Clear ownership: Let BI authors, developers, and business owners evolve their parts independently within one consistent destination. Business context: Organize navigation and branding around the process, not the underlying technology or workspace. Get started Build the tailored experience with Fabric Apps , then use the org app guidance to package it with Power BI reports and other supported Fabric content. Build the experience users need with Fabric Apps. Distribute it in the context of their work with org apps.

title: From a prompt to an operational dashboard: Generate Real-Time Dashboards with Copilot (Preview)
text: Start with the question, not a blank dashboard Which transit stations are sending the most fans toward a stadium? How does that incoming demand compare with activity at the gates? Where are queues building? Answering these operational questions traditionally requires translating them into tables, queries, visualizations, and a dashboard layout. When you already know what you want to monitor, that setup can get in the way of the question you are trying to answer. Copilot in Microsoft Fabric can generate a Real-Time Dashboard from a natural-language description of the insights you want. Working with a selected database in an Eventhouse, it uses the tables in that database to create a dashboard tailored to your goal. Figure: Start generating a Real-Time Dashboard with Copilot from an Eventhouse database . Rather than beginning with an empty canvas and building each visual separately, you describe the operational view you need. Copilot helps create the initial dashboard, and you review and customize it for your team. Describe, refine, and create Copilot can already help you write KQL queries and edit individual dashboard tiles. With dashboard generation, you can start one level higher: describe the operational view you need and let Copilot bring several related insights together into an initial dashboard. Copilot works from the context you provide about the dashboard you want to create. Describe the operational goal first, then add the details that matter for the view you have in mind. For example, specify the signals you want to monitor, the comparisons that are important, and any tables you know are relevant. You can also describe how you want the information organized. You might ask for an overview of the most important measures together with trends over time and breakdowns by location. You don't need to define every tile before you start. Use follow-up messages to clarify the request as Copilot develops the dashboard plan. Before creating the dashboard, review how Copilot has interpreted the request. This gives you an opportunity to narrow the scope, emphasize a particular comparison, or add context that was missing from the original prompt. From your Eventhouse, open New Real-Time Dashboard and select Generate with Copilot (Preview) . In the Copilot pane, describe your goal, the data you want to prioritize, and how you want the dashboard organized. Data-specific example prompts can help you get started. Figure: Describe the operational insights you want in the Copilot pane. The experience is conversational. You can follow how Copilot interprets your request and use follow-up messages to refine the scope or focus before creating the dashboard. For example, you might clarify which tables matter or ask to emphasize comparisons between locations instead of an overall summary. When you're ready, select Start dashboard creation , choose a dashboard name and workspace location, and select Create . The result is a Real-Time Dashboard you can continue to edit, not a static image of suggested charts. Figure: Choose a name and workspace for the generated Real-Time Dashboard Example: Connect transit arrivals with stadium gate load Consider a stadium operations team preparing for an event. Transit arrivals provide one view of incoming demand, while gate activity and queue lengths provide another. Looking at those signals together helps the team understand where to focus its attention. In this example, the prompt points Copilot to the relevant transit, stadium gate, stadium zone, and match-event data. It asks for estimated passengers and fans heading to the stadium, broken down by station and transit line, alongside gate entries and queue lengths. The goal is specific: compare incoming transit demand with activity at stadium entrances. That level of context makes the desired analysis concrete. The goal isn't simply to visualize every available column. It's to compare people arriving by transit with activity at the stadium entrances. The generated dashboard brings several views together: Summary tiles for estimated transit passengers, fans heading to the stadium, the relationship between those totals, and average gate queue length. A comparison of transit demand and gate entries over time. Passenger breakdowns by station and transit line. Gate-level and zone-level comparisons of transit inflow and gate activity. A detailed table of current gate load and queues. Together, these views give the team an overview and a way to inspect individual locations. A summary can suggest where to look next; a station breakdown or gate table provides more detail for that investigation. As with any generated dashboard, review the result before relying on it for operational decisions. Verify the queries, relationships between the data, and the meaning of the measures to make sure the dashboard represents the intended analysis. Make the dashboard your own An initial dashboard gives you something concrete to evaluate. Are the most important measures easy to find? Does each chart answer a clear question? Would a different visual make a comparison easier to understand? After generation, you can change visual types and modify the queries behind the tiles. Copilot can also help with editing visuals or writing queries as you refine the dashboard. Figure: The generated dashboard combines transit demand, gate activity, and queue information. Next steps Explore Generate Real-Time Dashboard using Copilot for the workflow and use Copilot's feedback controls to share what works and what needs improvement. Learn how to further Customize Real-Time Dashboard Visuals to make this dashboard your own.

title: Strengthening data security with workspace-level private connectivity for custom endpoints for Eventstream (Preview)
text: Organizations that operate sensitive applications often keep them in networks with no route to the public internet. Applications in restricted networks need real-time analytics without a route to the public internet. Eventstream now supports workspace-level private links for custom endpoint sources (Preview), so those applications can send events to Microsoft Fabric over a private connection. Teams can bring sensitive operational data into real-time analytics without opening a public internet path for ingestion. The change is especially useful for in-house applications, services, and gateways that do not have a managed Eventstream connector. They can publish directly to a custom endpoint source through the workspace’s private connection, bringing these workloads into the same private networking model as supported connector-based sources. What is workspace-level private connectivity? Private Link is a network security feature of the Fabric platform that provides a private connection between a virtual network and Fabric. Data traffic travels over the Microsoft backbone network instead of the public internet. Workspace-level private links map an individual workspace to a virtual network, which makes it possible to restrict access to specific workspaces while other workspaces remain open to public access. Each workspace has its own private link service, and that service can accept connections from multiple virtual networks through separate private endpoints. In the other direction, a single virtual network can connect to multiple workspaces by creating a private endpoint for each one. To reach a workspace over its private link, applications use a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) that is constructed from the workspace ID. When the FQDN resolves inside a virtual network that has a private endpoint for that workspace, it returns a private IP address, and the connection stays on the private network. Eventstream integrates with workspace-level private links. When a private link is in place and public access is restricted, an eventstream in that workspace can be reached only from approved virtual networks. This means that any source sending data into the eventstream must communicate through the private link rather than over the public internet. Why custom endpoint support matters Eventstream provides managed connectors for sources such as Azure Event Hubs, Azure IoT Hub, Apache Kafka, MQTT, and database change data capture (CDC) sources. For an application without a managed connector, a custom endpoint source provides connection information for publishing events directly to an eventstream. Applications, services, or gateways can publish using supported Kafka or AMQP clients, or Azure Event Hubs SDKs. In-house applications can run in restricted network segments where access to the public internet isn't permitted. Before this release, a team in that position had to allow a route to the public internet or keep the application outside of Eventstream. With private link support for custom endpoints, these applications can publish through a private endpoint, and the organization's network policy remains in place. Workspace-level vs. tenant-level protection Tenant-level private links provide private connectivity across a Fabric tenant. When public internet access is also blocked at the tenant level, supported workspaces and resources are reachable only through private connections. That scope suits organizations that require a tenant-wide restriction. In a mixed environment, however, some workspaces contain sensitive operational data while others need standard internet access. Blocking public access tenant-wide can prevent those legitimate access patterns and add administrative overhead. Workspace-level private links address this by allowing protection to be scoped to individual workspaces. A security team can restrict the workspaces that hold regulated or operationally sensitive data while leaving the rest of the tenant’s workspaces open to public access. Each decision is independent: adding a private link to one workspace does not affect any other workspace. This makes workspace-level protection a better fit when the sensitivity of the data varies across teams, projects, or business units within the same tenant. How the components fit together A custom endpoint source and an Azure private endpoint serve different purposes: one receives events inside Eventstream, while the other provides the private network path. The workspace private link service connects that path to the target workspace. The workspace private link service is a Fabric-side resource that maps a specific workspace to the Azure Private Link infrastructure. It is what makes a workspace eligible to receive private connections. Each workspace has its own private link service, and it is the anchor point that private endpoints connect to. An Azure private endpoint is a network interface inside the customer’s virtual network. It is created in Azure and connected to the workspace’s private link service. Once in place, the private endpoint provides a private IP address that routes traffic from the virtual network to that workspace over the Microsoft backbone network. Multiple private endpoints in different virtual networks can connect to the same workspace, and a single virtual network can host private endpoints for multiple workspaces. The custom endpoint source is the application-facing entry point inside Eventstream, not an Azure networking resource. It supplies the connection information an application uses to publish events with supported Kafka or AMQP clients, or Azure Event Hubs SDKs. With a workspace-level private link configured, the application’s traffic reaches that source through the Azure private endpoint over the Microsoft backbone network. This keeps the application-to-Eventstream ingestion path off the public internet. Feature in action: A telecommunications example Consider an illustrative scenario: a telecom operator monitors a mobile network with thousands of cell towers and connected devices. Each reports its status continuously. Faults, such as a tower losing power or a connection between sites going down, send messages to an in-house monitoring application running in the operator’s private network. The operations team needs to see these faults within seconds to respond before more customers lose service. In this scenario, governance policies prohibit public internet access from the monitoring application and require the receiving Fabric workspace to reject public traffic. Without a supported private ingestion path to the custom endpoint, the operator in this scenario would need another way to deliver events. Opening a public internet route would require an exception to its network policy. A scheduled batch process could delay fault visibility, while a separate middleware layer would add infrastructure to maintain. The value of private custom endpoint support is avoiding a public-access exception or an additional relay solely to reach Eventstream. With workspace-level private links configured, the monitoring application can send fault messages to the eventstream’s custom endpoint source through an Azure private endpoint, without crossing the public internet or using an additional relay solely for public network access. Eventstream can route the messages to an Eventhouse in preprocessing mode for querying live data by town or region. A cluster of tower faults can indicate a regional outage and help operations investigate while the incident is developing. A second copy can go to a Lakehouse for long-term analysis, where engineers can study months of fault history to inform capacity planning and maintenance schedules. How it works Before you begin, use a workspace assigned to a Fabric capacity (F SKU), enable the required workspace-level inbound network tenant setting, and confirm that you have workspace admin access and the necessary Azure permissions. title: Using Allow workspace settings editing policy in Fabric (Preview)
text: Your teams are ready to build. They know their data, understand their business, and need the freedom to manage the workspaces where ideas become solutions. As adoption grows, that freedom becomes even more valuable. So does the ability to protect the settings that matter most. A workspace admin role brings broad responsibility. But owning an analytics workspace shouldn't mean every administrator also needs authority over its encryption and networking. Organizations need a more precise way to share responsibility, without pulling everyday workspace management back into a central team's queue. At FabCon Barcelona, we introduced the Allow workspace settings editing policy, part of Microsoft Fabric policies, currently in preview. We're excited to give organizations finer control over sensitive workspace changes while keeping teams in charge of their day-to-day work. Now, you can delegate workspace ownership with clearer boundaries around who can change what, and where. Figure: Animated GIF - Configure and enforce network security through the Allow workspace settings editing policy. Put the right decisions in the right hands Fabric administrators can centrally define which workspace admins may edit supported settings, using conditions based on Microsoft Entra security-group membership, workspace, and setting type. The same organization can reserve some changes for a security team and delegate others to approved platform teams. We're starting with security-sensitive controls: customer-managed key encryption and outbound networking . Workspace admins keep their role and can continue managing unrelated workspace settings. An allow rule adds no new workspace privileges; users still need the workspace admin role to make these changes. That precision opens up practical ways to give teams more autonomy. Below are a few examples. Putting this to practice – Real scenarios from our customers Delegate workspace administration while retaining control of encryption Consider a bank that wants business teams to administer their own analytics workspaces. Its security team is reluctant to expand the workspace admin role because those users could also change customer-managed key settings. The Fabric administrator uses the policy to allow encryption edits only for workspace admins in an approved security group. The bank can then give more business users the workspace admin role without authorizing them to change that encryption configuration. Business teams handle everyday administration; the security team retains control of customer-managed key settings. Give development teams room to experiment A development sandbox and a production workspace serve different purposes. They shouldn't automatically need the same operating model. For example, an organization can allow workspace admins to edit outbound networking in designated development workspaces while reserving those changes in designated production workspaces for an approved platform group. Separate allow rules make those boundaries explicit. Developers gain flexibility where experimentation is expected. Production teams retain tighter control where a change can affect business-critical work. Administrators can reflect those differences in policy rather than impose the same restrictions everywhere. Bring networking decisions closer to the teams delivering solutions As Fabric adoption expands across business units, one central platform team can become the default destination for every networking request. Approved regional or business-unit platform teams may already have the expertise to take on some of that work. Fabric administrators can authorize those teams to edit outbound networking settings in specific workspaces, provided the people making the changes are also workspace admins. This creates a path to distribute administration as the organization grows. Qualified teams can handle changes within their assigned workspaces, while central administrators define and maintain the boundaries. Make the boundaries part of the workflow A governance decision has more value when the platform enforces it. Fabric evaluates the policy in the portal and through APIs, and records policy enforcement decisions in audit logs. Administrators can manage active policies centrally in the OneLake catalog's Policies center. The policy controls who can edit, giving organizations a way to enforce responsibility for future changes alongside their existing security and operational processes. Get started Choose a concrete scenario: reserve encryption changes for security specialists, or give an approved platform team control over outbound networking in selected workspaces. Identify the relevant workspace admins and security groups, then define the allow rules. Advanced mode uses an allow list: governed edits that match no rule are blocked. Plan every scenario you want to preserve across the tenant, including settings and workspaces outside your initial focus. Note that allowing encryption edits alone, for example, can block managed private endpoints edits unless another rule allows them. When your rules are ready, create and activate a tenant-scoped policy set . Validate both allowed and blocked scenarios with test accounts, and review the enforcement results before broader adoption. As more teams build with Fabric, governance needs to support that growth. Give people the freedom to own their workspaces, with sensitive security changes in the hands of the right specialists. That's how you make room for the next team and its next idea. Learn more about Allow workspace settings policy . We’re happy to hear any feedback you have about Fabric policies. To let us know what’s on your mind, fill out this form so we can better understand how policies are impacting your Fabric usage, what is working well, and what new policy capabilities would be most valuable.

title: Manage once, reuse everywhere: Introducing variable library support for Eventstream (Preview)
text: Moving a real-time data pipeline from development to test to production should not mean reconfiguring every source and destination. Yet environment-specific connection details and destination references can make each release a manual, error-prone task. Variable library integration with Eventstream in Microsoft Fabric lets teams reuse the same eventstream definition across environments, with references that resolve to each environment's resources. What's new? Variable library integration with Eventstream is available in preview. For supported source connections and destination items, you can use variable library references instead of direct values. These references are preserved through Git integration and deployment pipelines, helping teams reuse an eventstream definition across workspaces with environment-specific configuration. How variable library integration works Variable library is an item type in Microsoft Fabric that provides a centralized way to define and manage configuration values at the workspace level. Instead of entering environment-specific connection details and item identifiers directly into an eventstream, a team creates variables in a variable library and references them from the eventstream's source and destination configuration. The variable library supports two reference types relevant to Eventstream. A connection-reference variable points to a Fabric connection, such as the one used by an Azure Event Hubs or PostgreSQL CDC source. An item-reference variable points to a Fabric item, such as the KQL database for an Eventhouse destination or the Lakehouse that receives ingested data. Neither store credentials nor raw connection strings; both store pointers to managed Fabric resources. A variable library can contain multiple value sets, each representing a different environment. Figure: Variable library with item-reference and connection-reference variables configured across default and alternative value sets. A value set named "Development" might point a connection reference to a development Event Hub and an item reference to a development KQL database, while a value set named "Production" points both to their production counterparts. Only one value set is active at a time, and the eventstream resolves its references against the active set. Eventstream connects data sources to destinations inside Fabric. Each connection and destination is identified by environment-specific values: a connection ID, a workspace ID, an item ID. When an eventstream is promoted to the next environment, those values need to change. Without variable library integration, teams handle this manually: reconfiguring each source and destination after deploying to a new workspace, maintaining parallel definitions per environment, or running find-and-replace scripts against exported definitions. These approaches introduce risks such as: A missed replacement can route production data to a development database. A manual edit during a release can introduce downtime. Variable library integration moves environment-specific values into a centrally managed variable library. The eventstream definition stores symbolic references to those variables, allowing the same definition to be used across environments. During deployment, the target workspace’s variable library supplies the values for its local resources. Portability depends on how the variable library is configured in the target workspace. The eventstream definition retains its symbolic references, while the target workspace’s variable library maps those references to the managed connections and items used in that environment. These can include an Event Hub connection, KQL database, or Lakehouse, without embedding credentials or raw connection strings in the eventstream definition. Each environment provides its own values for the same variables. For example, SourceConnection can point to a development Event Hub connection in the development value set and a production Event Hub connection in the production value set. These symbolic references are preserved when the eventstream definition moves through Git integration or a deployment pipeline. Before deploying and publishing the eventstream, the target workspace’s variable library and active value set must be configured so that the references resolve to the intended resources. Example: Promoting a logistics eventstream Consider an illustrative logistics scenario: GPS devices on fleet vehicles send location and status events to an event hub in Azure Event Hubs. An eventstream routes those events to a KQL database in an Eventhouse for live fleet dashboards. The engineering team maintains development, staging, and production environments, each with its own event hub and KQL database. Before variable library integration, promoting the eventstream from development to staging required deploying the definition and then manually updating the Event Hub connection and KQL database reference in the staging workspace. A missed update during one release could cause staging events to flow into the development KQL database, corrupting test results and delaying the release. With variable library integration, the team creates a variable library in each workspace containing a connection-reference variable for the Event Hub connection and an item-reference variable for the KQL database. In each workspace, the active value set points both variables to that environment's resources. The eventstream definition uses symbolic references to these variables rather than direct identifiers. When the team promotes the eventstream through a deployment pipeline, the definition arrives in the staging workspace with its symbolic references intact. With the staging workspace's variable library configured for staging resources, those references resolve to the staging Event Hub connection and KQL database. The team does not need to edit those identifiers in the eventstream definition, reducing the risk of routing data to the wrong environment. Configure an eventstream to use variable library references Configuring an eventstream to use variable library references follows a short sequence. Create a variable library in the workspace and add the variables the eventstream will reference. In the eventstream's source configuration, select Use a variable in the connection field, then choose the connection-reference variable from the variable library. In the destination configuration, turn on Use variable for the destination item selection and choose the item-reference variable. Publish the eventstream and confirm that the source and destination resolve correctly and show an active status. To support multiple environments, add value sets to the variable library, one per environment, and configure each with the connection and item values for that environment. Set the appropriate value set as active in each workspace. Before promoting the eventstream, ensure that the target environment's source connection and destination item exist and are accessible. Deploy the variable library to the target workspace, configure its values for those resources, and select the appropriate active value set. Then deploy the eventstream and verify that its symbolic references resolve against the target workspace's variable library. For the complete setup procedure, including prerequisites and troubleshooting, refer to Variable library integration with Eventstreams . Benefits Variable library integration gives teams a structured way to manage the relationship between an eventstream and its environment-specific resources. The most immediate benefit is a reduction in deployment risk. When connections and destinations are expressed as symbolic references, promoting an eventstream to a new workspace does not require anyone to find and replace environment-specific identifiers. The values change because the target workspace's variable library supplies them, not because someone edited the definition. This reduces the risk of deployment er

title: Bringing Rust-native Spark compatibility to Microsoft OneLake with Sail and LakeSail
text: Coauthor: Shehab Amin Microsoft OneLake gives every Microsoft Fabric tenant a single, unified data lake built on open formats. One copy of data, many engines: that is the promise, and it is what makes OneLake such a strong foundation for analytics and AI alike. This post looks at how Sail , the open-source distributed compute framework, and LakeSail Cloud , the managed platform for running Sail in production, connect natively to OneLake, and what that unlocks for teams running Spark and Python workloads on Fabric. Sail is a drop-in replacement for Apache Spark, rebuilt from the ground up in Rust, with Rust-native support for Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg out of the box. That makes it a natural fit for OneLake, where lakehouse tables are stored in exactly these open formats. Point Sail at a Fabric lakehouse and it reads and writes the same tables the rest of Fabric uses, with no data copies, no extra connectors to install, and no changes to existing Spark code. One engine for data and AI Sail implements the Spark Connect protocol, the gRPC interface that decouples Spark clients from the engine that executes their plans. Existing Spark SQL and DataFrame code targeting Spark 3.5 or 4.x runs as is from any Spark Connect client, whether PySpark, Scala, Go, or Rust. The only thing that moves is the connection string. Before switching the endpoint, however, check the workload’s APIs, UDFs, and dependencies against Sail’s supported features. from pyspark.sql import SparkSession spark = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://sail-host:50051").getOrCreate() Behind that familiar interface sits a very different engine. Sail is written entirely in Rust with no JVM. Data stays in Apache Arrow columnar format end to end; query execution builds on Apache DataFusion with vectorized SIMD kernels, and an async actor runtime coordinates distributed work without locks. For teams adding AI steps to data pipelines, Python execution overhead can become a bottleneck. Apache Spark runs Python UDFs in separate worker processes, requiring data transfer across a process boundary. Sail removes that boundary entirely: It embeds the Python interpreter in the engine, allowing Arrow-native UDFs to share Arrow buffers with query execution. This avoids that inter-process transfer, Python becomes a native part of the execution plan rather than a detour out of it, which matters for AI workloads, where heavy lifting so often happens in Python. The same engine runs in two deployment modes. On Kubernetes, it runs as a distributed cluster for production scale. On a single node, whether a laptop or one large VM, it is a great fit for local development, testing, and smaller datasets, and it works out of the box on Windows, macOS, and Linux: with no JVM to install or configure, a pip install is the whole setup. Either way, a Sail server starts in seconds, and its workers are stateless and lightweight, so a cluster can scale out quickly when load arrives and back down to zero when it passes. LakeSail’s derived TPC-H benchmark compared Sail 0.7.0 with Apache Spark 4.2.0 using 22 queries over 100 GB of raw data stored as Parquet on the same AWS EC2 r8g.4xlarge host. Sail completed the queries in 52.81 seconds versus 534.78 seconds for Spark, with reported per-query speedups ranging from 176% to 2819%. Peak memory usage was 26 GB for Sail and 72 GB for Spark; shuffle spill to disk was 0 GB and about 115 GB, respectively. LakeSail modeled a nearly 98% compute cost reduction by combining shorter runtime with an assumed move to a smaller instance, with memory treated as the dominant sizing and pricing factor. That estimate is not a measured OneLake workload saving. Evaluate your own pipelines to establish performance and cost in your environment. The workloads this serves The integration is aimed at patterns that will look familiar to most data teams on Fabric: Scheduled ETL. Nightly PySpark jobs that transform raw orders, events, or clickstream data into curated tables in a lakehouse. The code already exists; the goal is to run it faster and cheaper without a rewrite. Interactive exploration. Analysts and engineers query production-scale tables from a notebook or IDE, where a tight iterate-and-refine loop matters more than anything. AI enrichment. Generating embeddings over product reviews for semantic search, classifying support tickets with a language model, or running feature engineering that goes beyond built-in SQL functions. These steps live in Python, and they increasingly sit in the middle of ordinary data pipelines rather than off to the side. Agent-driven analytics. AI agents that explore tables, run queries, and validate results on a person’s behalf. Sail ships an MCP server so agents can query lakehouse data conversationally, plus a one-shot CLI : pipe a PySpark script into sail spark run and a local server starts instantly, executes the script, and shuts down when it finishes. The Sessions capability covered below gives each agent its own scope, revocable access to real compute. These workloads share a practical goal: use existing Spark and Python skills to transform OneLake data without maintaining a separate stored copy. Sail brings SQL and Python execution into one engine, reducing the need to move between runtimes as AI steps enter the pipeline. Try Sail open source with OneLake To try the OneLake example, use a test lakehouse and a Microsoft Entra identity with permission to read the source tables and write the output table. Install Sail and a compatible PySpark Spark Connect client before running the script : pip install "pysail" Sail ships a OneLake catalog provider that talks to OneLake’s open table APIs. It supports two modes: iceberg, which uses the Iceberg REST catalog endpoint, and delta, which uses the Unity Catalog-compatible Delta metadata endpoint. For the full list of supported authentication methods, see the OneLake catalog guide in the Sail documentation. The example below turns order data in OneLake into daily revenue by region and writes the result back for downstream analysis. It authenticates with Microsoft Entra ID, registers the lakehouse as a catalog, and connects PySpark to an in-process Sail server. Replace the sample credentials and workspace/lakehouse.Lakehouse location with your test environment’s values. A lakehouse named sales in the analytics workspace uses analytics/sales.Lakehouse; tables in a schema-enabled lakehouse use dbo by default. import os from pysail.spark import SparkConnectServer from pyspark.sql import SparkSession # Authenticate with a Microsoft Entra service principal os.environ["AZURE_TENANT_ID"] = " " os.environ["AZURE_CLIENT_ID"] = " " os.environ["AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET"] = " " # Register the lakehouse as a catalog named "fabric" os.environ["SAIL_CATALOG__LIST"] = ( '[{type="onelake", name="fabric", url="workspace/lakehouse.Lakehouse", api="iceberg"}]' ) # Start a Sail server in-process and connect to it server = SparkConnectServer() server.start() _, port = server.listening_address spark = SparkSession.builder.remote(f"sc://localhost:{port}").getOrCreate() spark.sql("SHOW TABLES IN fabric.dbo").show() orders = spark.table("fabric.dbo.orders") daily_revenue = ( orders .groupBy("order_date", "region") .sum("amount") .withColumnRenamed("sum(amount)", "revenue") ) daily_revenue.write.format("iceberg").saveAsTable("fabric.dbo.daily_revenue") The script writes a native Iceberg table to OneLake. Fabric workloads can consume supported Iceberg tables through OneLake’s metadata virtualization. Validate the output in the Fabric portal and in the downstream experiences you plan to use, including Power BI through Direct Lake, Fabric notebooks, and the SQL analytics endpoint. To use the Delta Lake path instead, set the catalog API to delta and use a Delta Lake-compatible writer; changing the catalog setting alone does not change the output format. AI enrichment with Arrow Python UDFs Python user-defined functions (UDFs) let teams add custom transformatio

title: Access versioned lakeFS data from Microsoft Fabric with Microsoft OneLake shortcuts
text: Coauthor: Iddo Avneri (Treeverse) Use a live branch for up-to-date analytics or pin a shortcut to an immutable commit when reproducibility matters. Data teams often need two seemingly conflicting things: immediate access to the latest data and the ability to return to the exact data behind an earlier analysis, report, or experiment. Maintaining both typically means creating snapshots, copying datasets, or building additional pipelines. That adds operational overhead and makes it harder to know which version of the data was used. Microsoft OneLake and lakeFS provide a simpler, complementary pattern for addressing this use case. OneLake shortcuts allow Microsoft Fabric lakehouses to reference data in external storage through a unified namespace. Because lakeFS exposes versioned data through an S3-compatible gateway , Fabric can access lakeFS-managed datasets by using a OneLake S3-compatible shortcut. The result: Fabric users can access either the current data on a lakeFS branch or an immutable version from a specific commit. This removes the need to create and maintain a separate pipeline for copying versioned data. Figure: Access lakeFS data from Microsoft Fabric using shortcuts to either a live branch or a pinned commit. Live data and reproducible snapshots A lakeFS repository organizes data using branches and immutable commits. A branch, such as main, advances as new data versions are committed. A commit identifies a specific repository state and remains unchanged. This makes it possible to create different OneLake shortcuts for different purposes: A branch-following shortcut gives Fabric users access to the current state of a dataset. A commit-pinned shortcut provides a stable snapshot for a report, experiment, audit, or other reproducible workload. A Delta table shortcut exposes a lakeFS-managed Delta table through the Fabric lakehouse and SQL analytics endpoint. All three shortcuts access the same lakeFS repository, but each provides the data contract appropriate for its workload. How the integration works You can connect Fabric to the lakeFS S3-compatible endpoint with scoped access credentials, then configure the shortcut to reference the required repository version and path. The lakeFS repository is addressed as the S3-compatible bucket. A branch name, commit ID, or tag identifies the desired version. The remaining path identifies the files or Delta table to expose in Fabric. For example, a Fabric lakehouse could use separate shortcuts for current data, a reproducible snapshot, and a Delta table: lakefs-current-data, pointing to a dataset on the main branch. lakefs-reproducible-snapshot, pointing to a specific lakeFS commit. lakefs-delta-table, pointing to a Delta table on main. Files can be accessed through the lakehouse’s Files area. A Delta table shortcut created under Tables can be queried through the Fabric SQL analytics endpoint. The data remains managed and versioned in lakeFS, while Fabric users access it through the environment and analytics experiences, they already use. What we validated We validated this pattern end to end using the official Microsoft Fabric REST APIs. Based on our testing, we arrived at the following conclusions: Fabric successfully connected to the lakeFS S3-compatible gateway. We created shortcuts to both a lakeFS branch and a specific lakeFS commit. After committing new data to main, the branch-following shortcut reflected the updated state. The commit-pinned shortcut continued to return the original, byte-identical data. A shortcut to a Delta table was recognized in the Fabric lakehouse and could be queried through the SQL analytics endpoint. In the validated configuration, Fabric could read data through the shortcuts but could not write changes back to lakeFS. Figure : Compare live branch data with a commit-pinned snapshot in Microsoft Fabric. Figure : Query lakeFS data directly from the Microsoft Fabric SQL analytics endpoint. Where this pattern helps Consider a team producing a recurring risk report. The data engineering team publishes new data versions to the main branch in lakeFS. The report can use a branch-following OneLake shortcut to access the latest published data in Fabric. When the report is finalized, the team can record (or create a shortcut to) the exact lakeFS commit used for that reporting period. Even after main advances, the pinned shortcut continues to expose the original data version. The same pattern can support: Reproducing an earlier analysis or model result. Providing auditors with the exact data used for a report. Comparing the latest dataset with a previously approved version. Giving different Fabric workloads stable or continuously updated views of the same source data. Reducing the number of copied snapshots and custom synchronization pipelines teams need to maintain. Getting started To use this integration pattern: Make the lakeFS S3-compatible gateway accessible from Microsoft Fabric. Create an S3-compatible connection in Microsoft Fabric using the lakeFS endpoint and scoped access credentials. Create a shortcut to the appropriate lakeFS repository, reference, and path. Use a branch reference for continuously updated data or a commit reference for a fixed, reproducible snapshot. For Delta data, create the shortcut under Tables so the table can be queried through the Fabric SQL analytics endpoint. Microsoft’s current S3-compatible shortcut documentation specifies access-key and secret-key authentication. Credentials should therefore be scoped and managed according to the organization’s security requirements. Access current and reproducible versions of data in Fabric OneLake shortcuts make externally managed data accessible across Microsoft Fabric without requiring a separate copy and staging workflow. lakeFS adds the ability to choose precisely which version Microsoft Fabric sees. Together, OneLake shortcuts and lakeFS let teams analyze the latest published data while retaining immutable data versions for reports, experiments, and audits. Teams can support both current and reproducible analytics in Fabric without maintaining separate data-copy pipelines. Learn more Create an Amazon S3 compatible shortcut in Microsoft Fabric lakeFS S3-compatible gateway documentation

title: Introducing the data engineering agent for Fabric (Project Osmos)
text: AI coding assistants are excellent at turning natural-language transformation instructions into code. For data engineers, the harder question is whether that code produces results they can trust. You can describe transformation logic in natural language, and an AI coding assistant will happily generate hundreds of lines of Spark code. Impressive. But a Spark job can execute successfully and still produce completely wrong results. The logic may work for a subset of the data but fail when run against the full dataset. The pipeline's logic and validation checks may not account for future changes to the data or schema. Incremental loads can cause duplicates. Revenue numbers might look perfectly reasonable until someone reconciles them against the source. Anyone who's spent time working with real-world enterprise data knows that automating data engineering with AI comes with a unique set of challenges. Data engineering involves more than code: it requires working with large datasets and retaining context about their schemas, relationships, and business rules over time. Quality & governance matter a lot. The cost of errors or data loss is very high. Data engineering work typically spans team-based, collaborative, long-running, milestone-driven projects; not a single conversation between one person and a coding agent. What if specialized, data-aware agents could help teams investigate these problems, implement solutions, and validate the results—not just generate code? Following Microsoft's acquisition of Osmos in January 2026 , we've been working on bringing autonomous data engineering capabilities as a native experience in Microsoft Fabric. The idea behind Project Osmos is simple: instead of asking AI to help you write data engineering code, you define a complete problem and the outcome you expect. It has the autonomy to use the tools and an orchestration framework to build, validate, troubleshoot, and refine its implementation, making decisions within the boundaries you set and working towards a high quality output. The task's code execution and data operations run within your selected Fabric lakehouse. Real-world data engineering is rarely straightforward Let's take an insurance use case to illustrate the complexity. Imagine an insurance company consolidating policy and claims data from enterprise systems such as SAP, Guidewire, and Oracle, a common challenge in an industry that grows through acquisitions. The project also needs to ingest external datasets and user-generated data. The objective is to build a consolidated view of a claim, including its policy, coverage, and financial history. Sounds reasonable, until you start looking at the data. The same person, vehicle, or incident could have different IDs across systems. The same ID could also refer to completely different incidents across systems. Reconciling payments and ledger entries needs to be done with extreme caution. Discrepancies could result in overpayments and wrong forecasts. You need to investigate the data, understand its relationships, establish the business rules, and validate that the resulting view is consistent with those rules. Getting it wrong can have serious downstream implications. Quality and accuracy matter more than speed. In this example, a team would ask the Project Osmos to investigate relationships across the datasets, implement the agreed business rules, and validate the consolidated claims view. The agent would autonomously work through the problem and regularly report updates to the user. Users can review the evidence and validate results before accepting the output. A purpose-built orchestrator Under the hood, Project Osmos uses a purpose-built orchestrator that coordinates multiple specialized agents to tackle the problem. Each agent has a well-defined role from code generation to validation to evaluation. The agents interpret instructions, analyze the data, evaluate implementation approaches, generate code in isolated sandboxes, and verify the outputs. They use execution results to guide further iterations, with the aim of meeting your validation and quality requirements. Your team reviews the evidence to determine whether the results are acceptable. Should the agent need additional information or get blocked, or if the agent determines that the task cannot be accomplished within the constraints, the user will be elicited for input and guidance, and task will pause waiting user input. Project Osmos isn't merely simulating what the code might do. It submits PySpark code through the Fabric Livy API for execution in Fabric Spark sessions, so it can test the implementation and validate actual results. Whether changes use copies, staging tables, or in-place updates depends on the write pattern you select. The goal isn't to remove humans from the process. It's to let the agents take on the investigation and implementation work, while allowing people to guide the outcome, resolve ambiguities, and review the evidence. Figure: Project Osmos coordinates knowledge, Spark worker, and validation agents in Fabric. Autonomy, with the right guardrails Of course, giving an AI agent the autonomy to execute code and modify data raises the most important question: How do you make sure it doesn't do something it shouldn't? Before a task starts, you review the operating guardrails recommended by Project Osmos to define the scope and impact of its work. You specify which resources it can use, where outputs should go, whether changes should be staged, how reruns should behave, and whether schema changes are permitted. Project Osmos also recommends a reasoning effort setting, which users can adjust. More extensive reasoning can be useful for complicated problems, but it also comes at the cost of additional time and compute. These instructions guide the agent's work, but they aren't a substitute for proper access controls. Agents operate within the user's permissions, and Fabric and OneLake permissions continue to enforce what the agent is authorized to access. And while Osmos can carry out extensive validation, your team ultimately determines whether the results meet the business requirements. A persistent task that lives in Fabric Real-world data engineering problems rarely get completed in a single sitting. Requirements change. New data arrives. Business rules get clarified. Often implementations that worked perfectly the previous month need to be revisited. With Project Osmos, work is organized into persistent tasks hosted in Microsoft Fabric. Each task represents an ongoing data engineering project, rather than a single chat exchange. Once created, a task runs independently in Fabric, consuming Fabric capacity units (CUs). You can start it from GitHub Copilot CLI, Claude Code, or Codex using the Skills for Fabric plug-in, then disconnect without stopping the work. You don't need to keep your terminal open, maintain an active chat session, or even keep your laptop running. The task maintains its state, context, execution history, and outputs. You can monitor its progress in your Fabric Lakehouse, inspect what the agents are doing, review errors, and examine the outputs. The task is reusable and can evolve with additional instructions. You can interrupt it to provide additional context, clarify a requirement, or pause and resume the work through your local coding agent. Say you've built a data pipeline, and a new data drop arrives the following week. You don't have to start another task and explain the entire project all over again. You can reference the existing task and ask Project Osmos to process the new data. It has the context of the previous work and can decide whether to reuse the existing implementation or update it to account for the new data. Figure: Animated GIF of a persistent Project Osmos task and its activity history in Fabric. Collaborative by design Complex data engineering projects are rarely a one-person job. They involve a team of data engineers, data architects,

title: Govern your Microsoft Fabric data estate from one place with the OneLake catalog and Govern Skills (Generally Available)
text: The Govern experience in the OneLake catalog is now generally available, providing centralized governance capabilities for tenants, domains, capacities, workspaces, tags, and policies in Microsoft Fabric. Govern Skills are also now available in the Skills for Fabric collection, giving AI agents the knowledge they need to help admins and data owners audit, investigate, and remediate governance issues at scale. Both were announced at FabCon Europe 2026. Together, they help you monitor, manage, and act on your data estate from one place, whether you work in the Fabric portal or with an AI agent. Why it matters As AI makes it easier for more people to build with data, data estates grow in size and complexity. More workspaces, items, and access requests create more decisions about ownership, organization, and protection. Centralized, proactive governance helps admins support new projects without turning every decision into a manual review or losing visibility into how data is used. Governance can't rely on periodic, manual audits anymore. It needs to be proactive, centralized, and able to scale with the estate. Capabilities with Govern experience and Govern Skills: Manage governance in one place instead of moving between separate admin settings, reports, and management pages. Understand your governance posture through estate-wide signals, gaps, and recommended next steps. Use AI-powered assistance to audit and remediate governance issues across many domains, workspaces, and items at once. Manage governance centrally in the OneLake catalog The Govern experience in the OneLake catalog brings management and administration together, so the people responsible for the data estate can see its state and act on it without leaving the catalog. The Govern tab provides two ways to focus your work: Tenant view - All data in Fabric page : assess the health of your entire data estate and use recommended actions to identify where to focus first. Owner view - My items page: focus on governance issues for items you can update. From either view, select View more to open the full insights report, explore governance trends, and see where gaps are concentrated. The following image shows the Govern experience in the OneLake catalog, with estate-wide insights, management capabilities, and recommended actions on a single page. Figure: Animated GIF - The Govern experience in the OneLake catalog brings estate-wide insights, management, and recommended actions together, so admins can see where to act first. The Govern experience also brings key management areas into the same place: Domain management : organize the estate around the way your business operates, manage domain ownership, and delegate responsibility to the right teams. Capacities: View and manage all capacities for your tenant. Workspaces : View and manage all workspaces in your tenant Policies Center (Preview): Configure, activate, and monitor governance policies across tenants, capacities, domains, and workspaces from one place. Policies in Fabric support attribute-based controls; for example, you can allow only a data engineering security group to create Dataflow Gen2 items in approved workspaces. Tags: View and manage existing tags or define data management tags for your organization. The following GIF shows how you move from the governance insights to managing domains, workspaces, and policies, all within the Govern experience. Figure: OneLake catalog Govern - a centralized experience for key management areas. Know where to act with governance insights Visibility is only part of governance. The Govern experience surfaces estate-wide signals, gaps, and recommended next steps, such as establishing sources of truth with endorsements or increasing Sensitivity label coverage. Instead of starting from a blank page, you start from a prioritized view of what matters most in your estate. Customize the governance report The insights behind View more are also available as a report in the Admin monitoring workspace, which every Fabric administrator can access. Its semantic model is curated for customization, so you can build your own reports on top of it, for example to add alerts, extra dimensions, or longer retention. The report is available to all tenants regardless of license or size, and admins can share it with others. Data owners get their own version of the report in My workspace. Figure: The OneLake catalog – Governance for Admins report gives admins analytics across health, curation, and protection, and can be extended through its semantic model. Govern with AI using Govern Skills Govern Skills are a collection of AI skills, available in Skills for Fabric , that help users assess, understand, and improve the governance posture of their Fabric environment. Rather than navigating reports, APIs, and admin experiences by hand, you can ask governance questions, investigate issues, and receive guided remediation recommendations through a conversation with an AI agent, such as GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code. Built on the OneLake catalog governance pillars Govern Skills align to the core governance pillars of the OneLake catalog: Health : keep the estate clean, active, and well organized. Protect : keep the estate safe and compliant. Trust : keep data understandable, discoverable, and trusted. What's included The initial set of skills covers all three pillars, with the broadest coverage in Health: Health: inventory the tenant, assess governance health, and detect empty domains, unassigned workspaces, inactive or unused items, and missing governance metadata. Health skills can also use Fabric admin APIs for actions such as bulk workspace-to-domain assignment and domain admin management. Protect : check sensitivity label coverage and domain default labels. Trust : check description, tag, and endorsement coverage, and identify which items to curate first. For every pillar, Govern Skills provide prioritized recommendations and remediation guidance. If a signal cannot be measured, the skill identifies the limitation instead of returning a potentially misleading result and directs you to the Govern tab or Microsoft Purview for review. A consistent operating model Each Govern Skill follows the same workflow: audit, explain, recommend, and remediate. Rather than returning raw data or a list of issues, each response includes the finding, supporting evidence, impact, priority, and recommended action. The skills also include guardrails. They use supported Fabric admin APIs, don't invent missing details, surface uncertainty, and request your confirmation before sensitive or destructive actions. The core idea: governance expertise, not just API access Giving an agent access to the Fabric admin APIs provides technical capabilities. Govern Skills add governance expertise, guardrails, and operating procedures to those capabilities. Govern skills provide an AI agent with the context a Fabric admin would use: the jobs to be done, the issues to investigate, the evidence to collect, the criteria for prioritizing findings, and the steps for remediation. This context reduces the agent’s need to infer governance practices, leading to more consistent results and a more focused path to completing each task. In short, Govern Skills turn governance expertise from something each model has to reconstruct into reusable knowledge provided by Fabric.
